Headline CPI rose to 0.8% YoY from 0.4% YoY and exceeded consensus expectations, while core CPI increased to 0.4% YoY from 0.3% YoY (Figure 2). Imported inflation accelerated sharply to 1.5% YoY from 0.0% YoY, while domestic inflation edged up to 0.6% YoY from 0.5% YoY. However, the broader message remains one of contained inflation pressures. Core inflation is still subdued, while the broader inflation mix remains consistent with price stability . R ecent comments from Schlegel suggest policymakers continue to view the latest inflation pickup as manageable rather than requiring a policy response in the near term. For CHF investors, the key question is whether supportive structural holdings are beginning to give way to weaker marginal demand. CHF remains a low-yielding funding currency and, in a constructive global risk environment, would normally be a natural candidate on the short side of carry trades. While positioning remains elevated, CHF holdings have gradually declined from a peak at the 86th percentile in April, to around the 77th percentile today. Flow dynamics are also becoming less supportive. The 5-day flow measure has turned slightly softer, while supportive 20-day flows have moderated from their recent peak (Figure 3). records.text: The magnitude of S&P 500 “over-earning” S&P 500 earnings grew by an extraordinary 51% year/year in Q2 2026 and have grown by 26% during the past four quarters. During the last 30 years, the recent pace of earnings growth has been exceeded only during the post-recession rebounds in 2010 and 2021. The recent strength of S&P 500 earnings growth has raised investor concerns that current earnings power is unsustainable and that the market is in an “earnings bubble.” S&P 500 earnings have recently outpaced both their historical trend and their historical relationship with US GDP growth. S&P 500 4-quarter EPS growth has averaged 7% during the past 30 years, and the relationship between S&P 500 earnings and US economic growth in recent decades would have pointed to a similar rate of earnings growth during the last few quarters. Tech and exporters continue to offer faster earnings growth compared to the broader market, supported by robust AI demand, overseas capex upcycle and market share gains. On the other hand banks stand out as an attractive diversification option, supported by higher payout ratios, improving revenue trends and cheap valuation vs global peers. Not a capex cycle, but an RRF led investment boost: Last but not least, there are no clear signs of a capex cycle in Italy, with overall GFCF growing in line with pre-pandemic standards. Even such growth is mostly the result of booming non-residential construction investment, which has risen by 107% since 2019. We have discussed the recent revisions made by ISTAT to the construction series within national accounts here. Much lower activity in housing post-Superbonus, has been fully compensated by an increase in activity in non-residential construction since 2023. We think this investment has risen mostly as a result of the implementation of the recovery fund. Data from ANCE, the Italian association of private construction contractors, shows a sharp increase in public construction projects, vastly related to the RRF. Yet, while the ANCE data prove an RRF led boost to construction activity, they do not justify in full the rise showed by national accounts data. At this stage, we are not able to explain in full the extent of this growth, and see risks of potential downside revisions to activity going forward. In general, a share of RRF money still remains on the table to be spent. However, we do not think the speed at which the spending has been growing can be matched going forward. That would represent an upside risk vs our forecast.

records.text: The name is bond — rethinking duration in balanced portfolios Risky bonds — YTD sell-off increases the drag since the COVID-19 crisis Global bond yields are near or above the pre-GFC highs owing to a combination of cyclical support, rising energy prices due to the Middle East war, crowding out from AI debt issuance and fiscal concerns. Concerns about stickier inflation and FX debasement have increasingly become a speed limit for central bank easing or even forced tightening, as in the case of the BoJ. While there has been a lot of focus on long-dated bond yields, some of the largest increases have been in the front end, with US 2-year yields up 120bp YTD, and increases have been led by real yields. This indicates a different regime with higher neutral rates and more competition for capital. The bond sell-off has extended the already prolonged period of weak bond returns that started after the COVID-19 crisis. Before the COVID-19 crisis long-dated bond yields were unusually low after years of negative rates and QE as central banks were fighting persistently low inflation and deflation risks, and they fell even further during the COVID-19 crisis. Following the sharp increase in inflation and aggressive central bank tightening, bonds had one of the largest drawdowns in history in 2022 – the 5-year rolling returns on US 10-year bonds were the worst in more than a century – in real terms they were nearly as bad as after WW1 and WW2 and in the 1970s (Exhibit 1). However, we have different regional views in terms of whether spreads would persist at such wider levels, or whether such a selloff would present a buying opportunity. In the US, we are more confident in future spread performance, even if they were to temporarily overshoot fair-value levels. The narrow but powerful AI capex cycle continues to buttress the US economy, generating rapidly rising revenues & profits, while other measures of cycle health such as early-stage US bank loan delinquencies and bank lending standards remain in fine health. Technically as well, the $IG market is materially better supported than the current consensus believes, with growth rates in net supply unremarkable vs. prior major issuance waves in 2015 & 2020. And with more attractive FX-hedged yields + rising European political risks (more on this later), we would expect more global flows to be re-directed toward $IG in the months ahead. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 14 September 2026 ‹#› STEER adds long EURHUF; remaining short GBPUSD OUR KEY VIEWS ▪ STEER adds long EURHUF amid widening dislocations due to rising oil prices and lower global equities. The model remains short GBPUSD ahead of the FOMC and BoE meetings this week, while it does not highlight any general USD mis-pricing into the Fed. ▪ EURUSD now appears slightly cheap while AUDUSD remains close to fair value, and USDJPY remains cheap. In Asia, the USD undervaluation has broadly reduced. ▪ The model closed its short USDILS position. ▪ Rising oil prices and declining global equities have led dislocations to increase selectively, with GBPUSD’s overvaluation rising to 2.4 z-scores after its fair value declined to 1.3262. The new regime also introduces a performance and compensation framework to prevent ‘herding’ caused by current peer benchmarking. Each generational fund will use a customized reference portfolio benchmark designed by AFPs, evaluated by tracking error and 36-month rolling returns. Performance that exceeds a tolerance band earns the AFP an additional fee, while underperformance requires it to compensate the fund. Performance within the band triggers no reward or penalty. The generational funds regime starts on 1 April 2027 (the current model remains in force until then). By 1 March 2027 administrators must submit their initial benchmark allocation (AFPs will be able to define their benchmarks for the different funds within broad ranges defined by the law). From 1 April 2028 to 31 March 2031 a special transition period will apply where performance bands are fixed at 33bp monthly (vs. 20–24bp after March 2031) and the maximum monthly tracking error is 1.3% (vs. 0.87% after March 2031). records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 the 2030s, Canada’s relatively favorable demographic profile should become an advantage again: working-age population growth remains positive even as it contracts across much of Europe and Japan. The opportunity is therefore to use the late 2020s to deepen the capital stock before labor supply becomes more supportive again. Canada’s next acceleration does not depend on a return to labor-led growth or to an export-driven model. It depends on whether mix of factors - a large but still concentrated capital pipeline, a more favorable demographic window and a more supportive policy regime - can lead to a self-reinforcing private investment and productivity cycle. In our view, this would shift Canada’s growth narrative from simply becoming a larger economy to a faster-growing one.

To determine the implications for the multiple, we grouped the curves into three growth environments: below trend (EPS 0 to 10%), above trend (EPS 10 to 20%), and hypergrowth (EPS above 20%). In a hypergrowth environment, when EPS growth came in above 20%, S&P 500 multiples were supported until ~24x where the 10y yield reached ~6%, whereas during above-trend growth of 10 to 20%, multiples were only supported up to ~20x with the 10y at ~5%. Today, equities trade at ~22x 2026 EPS estimates, which we see as defendable given the strong earnings cycle this year (adjusted 2026 earnings growth of ~28%). For 2027, the market is trading at ~18x consensus estimates and pricing in ~21% earnings growth on an adjusted basis (removing one-time charges from private investments). While the street is likely handicapping forward earnings projections due to ongoing geopolitical and macro uncertainty, history suggests the 2027 multiple still has room to re-rate higher, assuming earnings growth holds at 15%+. Similarly, we also see a historical relationship between valuations and yields across different productivity growth regimes (i.e., higher multiple support at a higher productivity growth). While this analysis is imperfect, as this cycle is unique (e.g., significant potential for AI driven productivity growth) compared to what we’ve seen historically, we do not think rates should pose a problem for equities at this stage. records.text: 14 September 2026 IG & HY Strategy Deutsche Bank AG Page 7 European Summary: Higher yields are turning from friend to foe. Spreads have remained remarkably resilient despite the rates sell-off, higher energy prices and weakening fund flows. But depressed total returns and the growing yield competition from other fixed income assets are starting to challenge the market’s goldilocks equilibrium. Broadly we still expect supportive yield-driven demand to be there. But a less attractive relative value proposal could still weigh on the scale of those inflows. In combination with a weakening European growth outlook and ample supply across €IG and €HY we expect that to lead to a moderate spread widening and decompression until year-end. In €IG, we still favour 6-7yr tenors to stay ahead of fixed-maturity fund demand that we expect to remain supportive. On an already beaten up 15y+ segment we remain broadly neutral but recommend to add in hyperscalers here. 10-15y valuations we consider more stretched and recommend to keep portfolio duration slightly below benchmark. On sectors, we still consider the margin recovery among some European cyclicals like Autos and Chemicals rather fragile and retain our generally defensive stance. That said, we fine-tune by moving Real Estate from MW to UW, Healthcare from MW to OW and retain our OW on Telcos despite recent headwinds. ETF flows data provides one signal in this respect: inflows into European long-term government bond funds have been lacklustre YTD, lagging significantly relative to the past four years. Meanwhile, short- term bond funds have seen exceptionally heavy inflows, as illustrated by Figure 7. The key point here is that investors have been dissuaded from taking duration risk in the current macro environment, instead preferring to deploy cash into shorter-duration securities. Alongside positioning pain in 10s30s swap steepeners, we think this dynamic has likely also contributed to the YTD cheapening pressures in long-end EGB ASWs. Can long-end EGB ASWs regain their composure? As with many other segments of the EUR rates complex, this question may hinge to a significant extent on energy market developments. A favourable outcome would see energy prices fall sharply on an eventual de-escalation in the Gulf, potentially encouraging investors to re-initiate 10s30s swap curve steepeners (and add duration risk in long-end EGBs). This backdrop would likely also enable several structural tailwinds that have struggled to gain traction this year to reassert themselves. Separately, Oman announced on Sunday evening that the meeting between the GCC countries and Iran planned for Monday has been postponed "in the interest of consensus". There is no new date for the meeting. We believe the prospect of the meeting that would have discussed the new framework for navigation via Hormuz had contributed to a slight pullback in oil prices late last week. records.text: al external debt issuance. Historically, September and October see substantial external debt issuance from local non-sovereign sectors (Figure 6). Following the significant above-average USD debt issuance observed in January and April this year, should the seasonal pattern materialize through September and October, we could see a larger-than-usual volume of external debt issuance from local entities. As corporates typically pay the long-end CLP cross-currency basis to hedge their USD liabilities, this potential increase in demand is expected to drive the CLP basis higher (Figure 7). Furthermore, a weaker USDCLP could encourage local corporates to increase hedging on their external debt, further driving up the CLP basis. Although the CLP may continue to face pressure in the medium term due to potential broad USD strength from Fed hikes, the current USDCLP level appears elevated, trading at a 2.2 z-score (~2.4%) above its MarFA fair value. Should USDCLP decline, the resulting increase in local hedging demand against existing external debt could push the CLP basis higher. Our proxy, using local real-sector FX derivative positions with local banks, confirms this: as USDCLP decreases, these positions tend to react with an increase in short CLP positions, thereby pushing the long end of the CLP basis higher. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 11 Country-perspective Germany | More strength from government investment expected: Growth has surprised to the upside in recent quarters. Between 4Q25 and 2Q26, GDP expanded by an average 0.35%Q, broadly converging toward the pace elsewhere in the euro area. This should raise growth to 1.1%Y in 2026 up from 0.3%Y in 2025, and we expect another small step up in 2027 (1.2%Y) (vs our previous forecast of 0.9%Y in both years). Looking at the drivers, net exports and government spending (investments in 4Q25 and consumption in both 4Q25 and 1Q26) have contributed to the recent uptick, while private consumption momentum was weak in 2026 and private investments remained a drag (Exhibit 29 and Exhibit 30 ). Going forward, we continue to expect positive export growth, albeit at a slightly lower rate, and we see scope for GDP impulses in public investments. On the former, we note that July brought a contraction and there is overall scope for some correction from the boost to chemicals demand that emerged due to supply issues elsewhere (see here). But production in ICT related industries has expanded and we expect that strong global demand and the capex build out will support exports in the coming quarters. Government investment in machinery and equipment (including defence) tends to accelerate in 4Q, which suggests more upside into year-end. However, it is important to note that higher rates are often symptomatic of stronger economic growth and robust demand for capital due to pro-growth policies, reflation, and boom cycles (dot-com in the 1990s, housing/EM in the 2000s, AI supercycle since 2023). Thus, higher rates more often do not translate into lower aggregate demand, and the revenue decline is far from sudden. While rates have risen in recent months, most consumer and corporate borrowing rates are still significantly below peak levels seen in 2023 (e.g., Bankrate fixed 30y is now 6.8% vs. 8.1% in 2023, High Grade Yields 6% vs. 6.5%, High Yield 7.7% vs. 9.6%). Additionally, this episode of higher rates is coming at a time when organic growth is arguably one of the strongest in history due to ongoing government deficit spending and an AI supercycle that continues to surprise to the upside. This is supporting resilience in consumption activity even amidst stubborn inflationary pressures and a k-shaped consumer. Nonetheless, it is hard to dismiss the unevenness of the economic recovery, with “higher-for-longer” rates crowding out consumer-related activity, housing and commercial real estate, capital-intensive industries not tied to the AI buildout, and highly levered companies and businesses. records.text: (3) Diversification benefits — from desperation to normalisation Equity/bond correlations are likely to be less negative compared with the post-GFC cycle but should start to decline from the elevated levels over the last 5 years. In the past 100 years negative equity/bond correlations have been the exception rather than the norm: only during the 1920s, the 1950/60s and since the late 1990s were equity/bond correlations consistently negative, as inflation was generally anchored (Exhibit 16). As a result, growth shocks were a more important driver of monetary policy. In the last 5 years equities and bonds have moved more in tandem, especially during the large combined drawdown in 2022. As we wrote before, with more inflation volatility and fiscal risks, we think equity/bond correlations will be closer to zero – we think bonds are increasingly becoming a tool for income generation but less for risk mitigation, similar to the 100 years before the late 1990s. records.text: h. Our long EURGBP idea also faces central bank risk this week. The ECB delivered its hike with some hawkish language, albeit from uncertain sources, while all BoE hikes are priced for after September. As we argue in Is the cart in front of the horse?, weaker labour market data and a less hawkish BoE tone point, on balance, to greater caution. If realised, GBP selling should resume, so we retain our long EURGBP position through this event risk and ahead of next month’s UK budget. The NOK and NEMO This leaves one new portfolio idea this week. Given the low probability of a hawkish Fed surprise and the growing disconnect between US yields and asset manager USD demand, we add a short USDNOK position. There are several reasons to express our tactical USD short against NOK. First, apart from JPY and GBP, it is one of the least crowded USD shorts (Figure 3). Second, Norges Bank is among the few central banks with clearly restrictive policy relative to its own estimate of neutral (Figure 4). The September meeting is priced evenly between a hike and a hold, but the bank’s transparent forward guidance means its projected policy rate path through the NEMO model could support still modest expectations of further tightening even if rates are unchanged. That greater transparency and certainty could attract a NOK premium while adding another oil sensitive currency to our view set. Admittedly, the equity/bond yield gap has declined in recent years owing to a combination of higher bond yields and Shiller P/Es rising to Tech Bubble levels (Exhibit 13). However, valuations are an even weaker signal for near-term equity performance. As we noted before, unlike during the Tech Bubble, today’s elevated cyclically-adjusted equity valuations are supported by high corporate profitability – the equity/bond yield gap is close to its long-term fair value based on 10-year inflation and GDP growth, as well as the S&P 500 return on equity (ROE). The path for equity valuations in the coming years will likely be determined by the impact of AI on S&P 500 profitability. In the near term, earnings growth and expectations for ROE are likely to remain the key driver of equity performance relative to bonds, more so than starting valuations. records.text: There are, however, important differences to the Tech sector today. The earnings of the banks were boosted by sharply rising leverage and the asset that they were financing – US real estate – did experience a valuation bubble. When the housing market collapsed, pushing economies into recession, it triggered a sharp fall in underlying earnings for the banking sector. There are important differences today. First, technology profits remain very robust, and balance sheets are strong overall. Second, interest coverage ratios for the aggregate S&P 500 and its median stock, for example, rank in the 99th and 68th percentiles relative to the past 20 years. Third, demand for compute is accelerating and outstripping supply; Microsoft recently declared their intent to triple data centre capacity in 6 years. The bottlenecks are increasingly power, land and data centre capacity rather than a lack of compute demand. At our annual Communacopia Technology Conference, Nvidia reiterated its 2030 AI TAM outlook to $3tn-$4tn and supply constraints continue to be broad based. Nonetheless, any slowdown in profit growth, in an environment of a much higher cost of capital, could put downward pressure on equity prices, reducing confidence in future cash flows across the ecosystem from the hyperscalers to the ‘pick and shovels’ that have been benefiting from the capex boom. 10. records.text: Liquid Insight | 14 September 2026 5 FX: USD limps into the FOMC The dollar remains subdued going into the September FOMC, despite implied pricing rising sharply to ~85% probability of a hike, post CPI. (Exhibit 7) Dollar sentiment has soured ever since Chair Warsh’s July FOMC press conference raised credibility concerns on lack of an articulated plan to address persistently above-target inflation. Since then, the market has received a mix of signals, including an attempted course correction from Chair Warsh at Jackson Hole (bullish), a strong August labor report (bullish), dovish comments from the Fed’s Williams and Waller (bearish), and the Treasury’s buyback gambit to suppress US yields (bearish). Beyond US economic and policy specific factors, the dollar has also been unable to rally amid the recent reacceleration in oil, gas, and refined energy products; something typically associated with dollar appreciation. Part of the puzzle lies in the broader re- pricing of central banks and curves globally. (Exhibit 8) Now with more than 3 hikes priced in for the Fed, the bar for this committee to “out-hawk” both expectations as well as other G10 central banks appears high. This is partly why despite the prospect of Fed hikes this year, we see the USD trading more-or-less sideways into year-end (ex-JPY) (see report: G10 FX back-to-school: dollar unloaded 08 September 2026). Estimating sentiment via returns, issuances and flows Our new EXD Sentiment Indicator combines six metrics drawn from fund-based positioning, primary market conditions and dedicated EM flow data. These components are intended to capture whether the market is demonstrating signs of crowding, fatigue or overly rich primary market conditions. Higher Sentiment Indicator readings are associated with near-term spread widening, while lower readings are associated with spread tightening. Each component was selected from a broader universe of candidates based on their independent contribution to predicting near-term spread movements. The final Sentiment Tracker value is simply the equal-weighted aggregation of those six components. The Buy or Sell designation is triggered when the value of the Sentiment Tracker is below -0.5 or above 0.5, respectively. The designation is an indication of strength of sentiment and should not be confused with recommendation to purchase any particular security. The EXD Sentiment Tracker is intended as one analytical input among many and is not intended to serve as a stand-alone investment strategy or recommendation. As a result, asset prices that are dislocated from their fair values are more likely than not to recouple with them. For MarFA Macro, our most used variant of the model, mispricings tend to unwind within one to four weeks. MarFA works on the basis that financial markets are statistically co-integrated, meaning that asset prices generally move together over time but can temporarily deviate from each other. records.text: 2 Natasha Kaneva AC (1-212) 834-3175 natasha.kaneva@jpmorgan.com Global Markets Strategy 17 September 2026 J P M O R G A N The answer depends less on how long the conflict lasts than on how the physical oil market continues to clear while it does. Commodities are physical markets. They have to clear, meaning supply and demand must balance almost in real time. Put simply, when supply exceeds demand, the surplus flows into inventories, signaling an oversupplied market and pushing prices lower. The opposite is also true. When demand exceeds supply, the shortfall is met by drawing down inventories. Stock draws signal a market in deficit, which tends to push prices higher. In other words, inventories are the key clearing mechanism between supply and demand. It is also why changes in OECD commercial inventories carry the largest weight in our oil pricing model. That logic sat at the center of our Illusion of Plenty thesis in April. Given the scale of the supply disruption, we expected inventories to draw rapidly and cautioned that, while the headline number looks considerable, the volume actually available to draw is far smaller. At the pace we anticipated—around 1.6 billion barrels—the drawdown would have pushed available stocks from 8.4 billion barrels at the start of the conflict toward operational floor levels by September. records.text: How to yield — asset allocation implications from rising bond yields The tactical and strategic case for higher bond allocations Higher bond yields support risk-adjusted returns for bonds in the medium term, but they are a less strong signal for near-term performance, especially relative to equities. On a tactical horizon the main drivers of optimal bond allocations are likely to be inflation momentum, the Middle East conflict and central bank policy, on the one hand, and the evolution of the AI boom with less of an earnings tailwind from AI capex, on the other. For longer investment horizons most of the variation of the bond vs. equity returns is still driven by equities – the increase in bond yields YTD is strengthening the case for higher strategic bond allocations compared to the last 5 years, when bonds had little value in portfolios, but this is mostly a normalisation back to the long-run optimal bond allocation range of 35-55%. In the near term, monetary policy and higher energy prices are likely to remain the key driver of both equities and bonds (Exhibit 20). As a result, higher bond allocations have added volatility rather than buffering portfolios. Further increases in bond yields are likely to weigh more on equities than bonds, in particular sharp ones due to energy prices or more aggressive central bank tightening – increases above 2sd over 3 months start to weigh more on equities (Exhibit 21). records.text: ab 14 September 2026 Global Research European Economic Comment SNB: What to expect on 24 September We expect no policy rate change on 24 September We expect the SNB to keep the policy rate at 0% at its upcoming meeting on 24 September, in line with market pricing. The key debate, however, remains when the SNB may increase its policy rate - in particular as the ECB seems set to raise rates further, as we now project. While we think a rate hike at the September meeting is unlikely, we do believe the risks for our baseline call for a June 2027 hike are clearly tilted towards an earlier hike, potentially followed by a sequence of hikes. So far, the SNB has signalled its intention - for example, through its inflation forecast - to remain on hold. In a recent interview, SNB board member Petra Tschudin noted the moderate Swiss inflation rates compared to other countries and referred to higher inflation abroad driving expectations of higher policy rates, which in turn should weaken the CHF. We believe this will also be the main message of the upcoming meeting - essentially we believe it is too early for the SNB to give a clearly hawkish impression as CHF weakness might still be welcome at this point. In our view, two aspects will be in focus on 24 September: (1) to what extent the SNB inflation forecast will change, in particular the slope and the end-point in Q2 2029 and (2) whether the SNB will modify its language on FX interventions. records.text: UK Insurance Ivan Bokhmat Barclays, UK What makes assets in your sector attractive today? The UK insurance sector has been at the forefront of industry consolidation with both domestic and international M&A. While a lot of consolidation in the life and personal non-life space has already taken place, in the more fragmented commercial/Lloyd's sector deal activity is likely to continue. North American alternative asset managers have continued to deepen their footprint in UK life and retirement, cementing 2025-26 as a watershed period for consolidation of the bulk annuity and retirement income space. Both Just Group (link) and Pension Insurance Corporation (link) were acquired by alternative asset managers this year, giving insurers access to enhanced private investment-grade credit origination. Alongside outright ownership changes, incumbents are increasingly opting for capability-enhancing partnerships rather than full disposals: Standard Life launched a UK PRT partnership with a CVC Capital Partners-led consortium including Prudential Financial, backed by up to £2bn of combined initial capital commitment, while Legal & General struck strategic global deals with Blackstone and Manulife to broaden reach across annuities, reinsurance and private markets. We read this as reflecting a bifurcation in strategy – asset-heavy North American capital seeking control of UK back-books and new business flow, versus UK incumbents choosing to retain balance sheets while importing origination

records.text: M Idea 50 Food Retail Marks & Spencer Group (MKS LN) Izabel Dobreva Rating: Overweight; Price Target: GBp 439/sh (Upside to PT: 16%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: We see an attractive long-term opportunity, with best-in-class market share gains across Food and Fashion, and strategic initiatives reshaping the long-term cost base of the business. Our FY28/FY29 EPS forecasts are 8-10% ahead of consensus on strategic turnaround and rebound in sales. The back-end 'hard wiring' of the business is still playing catch up vs. demand on the front-end, given standout products – we believe meaningful volume growth and profitability uplift can be unlocked if M&S can successfully modernise over the next 3 years. We see two main structural challenges currently: (1) The barriers to accessing M&S products need to be lowered holistically, through more and better stores, improved availability, and a stronger online experience. (2) There are significant investments needed in both capex/opex terms across DC automation and Digital in order to increase capacity and drive further share gains, which will act as a margin headwind near term. The good news however is that management has been forthright about these issues – there is a substantial £600mn cumulative savings programme in place, which brings mitigation, with FY27 likely to deliver >£100mn of savings. We think consensus is not crediting the paybacks of structural investments that will flow through over the next 3 years. For details

It highlighted little evidence of material second round effects so far, along with soft labour market conditions and tightening in financial conditions weighing on inflation. But there was a decisive hawkish shift compared to July, as we expected, in light of recent energy price moves. We interpret today’s decision as signalling that the BoE looks closer to moving towards tightening, if the recent rise in energy prices is sustained and barring big downside data surprises. Overall, the BoE is getting increasingly nervous about sitting out this shock entirely. Rising upside inflation and second round effects risks The BoE noted that risks to inflation were titled further to the upside compared with July and there is possibility of a less stark trade- off between growth and inflation. The MPC judged the shock as looking protracted with most members placing more weight on energy prices staying higher for longer in the absence of a lasting de- escalation. We provide a time-line the innovations and add-on feature that have been developed over last decade. The core model, meanwhile, has remained unchanged. MarFA’s innovations can be categorised into expansion of coverage, new methods connectivity and advanced analytics. MarFA has had positive performance since launch, but a decline of profitability in recent warrants further investigation. BNP Paribas MarFA provides the fair-value of asset based on the systemic information in the market. Deviations away from fair-value tends to be temporary and driven by idiosyncratic factors. As a result, asset price that are dislocated from their fair-values are more-likely-than-not to re-couple with them. For MarFA Macro, our most used variant of the model, mis-pricings tend to unwind within 1-4 weeks. MarFA works on the basis that financial markets are statistically co-integrated, meaning that asset prices generally move together over time but can, temporarily, deviate away from each other. These deviations are reflected in mis-pricings from MarFA fair-value, which we see as trading opportunities. MarFA was launched 10 years ago today. The model’s uniqueness comes from combining co- integration theory with Principal Component Analysis (PCA). records.text: Investment – Manufacturing capacity expansion The local capex response to the AI boom has arrived in Asia. Major manufacturers are poised to ramp up investment to expand production capacity in anticipation of sustained AI demand. Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC have all announced various investment projects to meet accelerating demand for high-end chips, and consensus forecasts imply capex for each of these firms will rise sharply into 2026 and beyond. We assess this trend via bottom-up aggregation of capital expenditures of listed Korean and Taiwanese tech companies. As a share of GDP , Korea tech capex is expected to rise by 1.1pp and Taiwan by 2.9pp in 2026 (Exhibit 7). However, headline capex should be heavily discounted when assessing its domestic growth contribution for two reasons. First, capex plans are generally global and do not necessarily contain a clear split between domestic and overseas investments. Company-level evidence from Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and TSMC4 suggests a substantial domestic bias, potentially reflecting efficiency gains from existing local semiconductor clusters. Parent-company PP&E purchases accounted for around 80% of Samsung Electronics’ total capex and over 90% of SK Hynix’s in H1 2026. The equivalent ratio for TSMC was also around 80% in 20255. records.text: In late July, we outlined our top-down framework for AI-related debt issuance n from the hyperscalers, using the CapEx estimates from our colleagues in GIR equity research as a key input. At the time, our estimate for 35% of 2027 CapEx to be financed with debt mapped to roughly $400 billion of gross debt issuance, globally, directly issued from the group. Several weeks later—and with the benefit of the most recent round of earnings n results—we refresh the gross hyperscaler issuance implied by our forecasts. We now expect $420 billion of gross debt issuance in 2027, which reflects some modest upward revisions in CapEx forecasts. This forecast would represent more than a 60% increase vs. our full-year 2026 n estimate of $250 billion of direct global hyperscaler IG debt issuance. So far this year, $229 billion has been issued across a range of currencies. We continue to expect 65% to 75% of the 2027 hyperscaler gross debt issuance to price in the USD IG bond market, subject to market conditions and investor receptivity in light of issuer concentration considerations. So far this year, we have tracked $578 billion of global, gross AI-related debt n issuance, which includes a broad universe of firms. Hyperscalers continue to represent ‘just’ 40% of overall AI-related debt issuance, underscoring the wide range of AI-related exposure in the global credit markets. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 The Inflation Data is Old News Last week's much-anticipated release of the latest inflation data was met with mixed reactions from various markets. First, bonds and stocks sold off early in the week as investors began to worry about hotter inflation data and higher for longer energy prices. After all, while Fed Chair Warsh has intimated he doesn't want the Fed to lead the markets anymore, one dynamic he has stressed is that the Fed will be resolute in getting inflation back to target after five years of missing that target to the upside. With the PPI coming in slightly hotter on Thursday, markets began to price in a higher CPI, with the 10-year yield approaching the psychologically important 5% threshold. Stocks sold off in sympathy as the probability of a rate hike at the September FOMC meeting reached ~70% ahead of Friday. With CPI confirming the trend, that probability quickly rose to ~90% into the weekend. Stocks rallied sharply on the news while bond yields held steady, illustrating once again that markets trade ahead of the headlines. As an aside, we think it also adds credence to Chair Warsh's commitment to re-establish free-market signaling. It's no secret the economy is booming at the moment, led by a generational capital spending cycle. records.text: Models are pre-built templates A model portfolio is a pre-built asset allocation – such as equities, bonds, mutual funds and cash – designed by an investment provider that financial advisers can use as a template for client accounts. Model portfolios are designed to meet specific investment objectives and risk tolerances, such as conservative, balanced or growth-oriented strategies. For example, a balanced model portfolio might recommend an allocation of 60% equities, 35% fixed income and 5% cash, providing advisers with a ready-made template. In practice, a model provider such as BlackRock, Capital Group or Vanguard constructs the portfolio and selects the underlying investments for each allocation sleeve. Financial advisers then implement the model across client accounts, directing capital into the funds and ETFs chosen by the provider. When the model is updated, advisers typically rebalance client portfolios accordingly, creating flows into new positions and out of those that have been reduced or removed. Model portfolios cut costs According to Morningstar data, model portfolios retain a fee advantage over unbundled mutual funds, arguably the fairest comparison, with savings ranging from 8bp to 40bp depending on the category (Figure 10). The gap is widest in more aggressive allocation strategies, where active management tends to be more expensive. The cost advantage stems largely from scale. Fiscal deficit has been systemically very high, exceeding 6% of GDP in FY2023, FY2024 and FY2026E. This is very unusual for the US economy that is expanding at near-trend rate. records.text: 1. There are two themes dominating our investor conversations: the impact of AI and the rise in interest rates. The two issues are linked as demand for capital from both the private and public sectors increase. In the private sector a surge in capex spending to fund AI infrastructure has eaten into free cash flow and forced companies to raise more in debt and equity markets. Meanwhile, government borrowing needs have increased as priorities shift towards upgrading critical infrastructure, energy security and defense at a time when cyclical inflationary pressures driven by higher energy prices are also resulting in higher policy rates. The combination has pushed up the cost of capital. As recently as 2022, for example, 30-year bond yields in Germany and Japan were close to zero (Exhibit 1). A rise in yields, together with more uncertainty (over geopolitics and the future impact of AI) have, in combination, pushed up the cost of capital. 2. This rise in yields comes after a near-record period of equity outperformance relative to bonds over 10-year holding periods (Exhibit 2). records.text: An Update on AI-Related Debt Issuance In late July, we outlined our top-down framework for AI-related debt issuance from the hyperscalers, using the CapEx estimates from our colleagues in GIR equity research as a key input. At the time, our estimate for 35% of 2027 CapEx to be financed with debt mapped to roughly $400 billion of gross debt issuance, globally, directly issued from the group. (Note: this excludes project finance issuance for data center and chip financing, which we forecast separately, expecting $300 billion in 2027). Several weeks later—and with the benefit of the most recent round of earnings results— we refresh the gross hyperscaler issuance implied by our forecasts. As Exhibit 1 illustrates, we now expect $420 billion of gross debt issuance, which reflects some modest upward revisions in CapEx forecasts. Our colleagues in GIR equity research have recently highlighted the ongoing supply-demand imbalance related to the AI build out and expect the CapEx cycle through the end of 2027 to remain elevated. This forecast would represent more than a 60% increase vs. our full-year 2026 estimate of $250 billion of direct global hyperscaler IG debt issuance. So far this year, $229 billion has been issued, across the range of currencies outlined in Exhibit 2. We continue to expect 65% to 75% of the 2027 hyperscaler gross debt issuance to price in the USD IG bond market, subject to market conditions and investor receptivity in light of issuer concentration considerations

records.text: M Idea 52 Household & Personal Products Haleon (HLN LN) Sarah Simon, Richard Li Rating: Overweight; Price Target: GBp 460/sh (Upside to PT: 38%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: As the only pure-play Consumer Health business in European Staples, Haleon offers access to leading brands in attractive categories (Oral Health, VMS, OTC), making it well placed to deliver sustainable mid-single-digit organic sales growth while expanding margins from FY26 onwards at a faster rate than most European Staples peers. We acknowledge weaker consumption trends leave less room to maneuver, but amidst an uncertain macro backdrop across categories, we expect Haleon to outperform European peers owing to its exposure to structurally attractive segments (particularly Oral Care), market-leading brands and a well defined cost-saving programme, which should boost both gross margins and reduce SG&A. All in, we see Haleon delivering a DD EPS CAGR for the next few years, with strong cash flow, which could support expanded buyback activity, or permit bolt-on M&A. Broader idiosyncratic drivers: Haleon is not an AI-driven story; rather, its Consumer Health portfolio provides structural exposure to broader Health & Wellness trends. Growing consumer focus on self-care and preventative health supports demand across Haleon’s core categories. records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 September 2026 ab 9 Figure 15: Current themes & drivers of US inflation Issue Our take 1. Crude oil price shock Retail gasoline prices peaked on May 20 and our baseline forecast relies on future curves that suggests most of the rise in prices since late February will be reversed by December. However, crude oil prices have been rising again and risks are skewed to the upside. (See Oil/Energy/Commodity prices later in this note for more detail.) 2. Broader supply shock Measures of supply stress moved up from February to May, but have, on balance started to retreat. Their rise is an upside risk to the projection, but the impact will likely be a small fraction of what occurred during the pandemic. (See the May US Inflation Monthly: Rising Supply Risks and the Supply and Relative Demand conditions section later in this note for more detail.) 3. AI adoption AI adoption is pushing up core PCE price inflation roughly 0.6pp currently, though less than 0.1pp for core CPI inflation. AI adoption likely to continue to push up inflation for next year before increased productivity growth pushes down inflation further out. (See essay 7 of the recent UBS Compendium for more detail.) 4. Tariffs Tariff impact on 12-month inflation has likely peaked, but there will still be moderate pass- through until early 2028. records.text: UK Economics 14 September 2026 Citi Research 5 situation, we would expect the Governor and at least two of his deputies to join the dissenters in voting for a hike. But the uncertainty bands around this call are large. It may happen earlier, or it may never happen at all. Everything is predicated on what happens in Hormuz, and the subsequent market reaction. This is a Committee that really does not want to hike, remember. Embedded in our assumption of a hike in Q4, is prolonged market volatility and energy price spikes. If the conflict hasn’t been resolved by November, it will have been going for a good part of this year, and it will have become very hard to argue these factors are transitory, pushing the MPC into action to assuage market concerns and preserve central bank credibility. The same rationale is also true for the hike we have in Q1, although that judgement is much more uncertain (we think it almost as equally likely that they would hold in Q1). By then, we will have a clearer sense of the extent of food price disruption from El Nino and the adverse climate. If, on the other hand, the conflict takes a pause or financial markets relax, then the Bank will feel vindicated in holding out and will, instead, just carry on holding. The stop-start nature of the war, together with other factors, such food import disruptions from El Nino, mean the inflation outlook is highly uncertain. Frequent policy pivots from the MPC, at the moment, should not, therefore, be surprising.

That helps explain why financial conditions remain easy and suggests that the drag on economic activity from these hikes is likely to be limited. Hence, one possibility is that the economy absorbs the tightening with little difficulty, prompting investors to continue to reassess the longer-run neutral rate higher over time, but this time with an even higher overnight rate. Although estimates of neutral have already moved up, they remain low relative to the economy's resilience. Under that scenario, the yield curve would likely bear-steepen. The alternative is that the Fed's higher near-term inflation forecasts create scope for downside surprises. If inflation undershoots the committee's projections, markets would likely scale back the hikes currently priced into the curve. The front end would be the main beneficiary, in our view. In short, while the paths differ, both point to a steeper curve rather than lower long-term yields. We therefore see attractive risk-reward in curve steepeners rather than in duration. We recommend 1yf 2s10s SOFR curve steepeners (entry -3bp). First one’s free : The Fed hike d rates by 25 bps as widely expected by the futures market, although we suspect that qualitative investor confidence was not as robust. They also signalled another rate hike this year, followed by a pause in the tightening cycle t hrough 2028. The SEP (while we still get it) shows a committee that is comfortable with a goldilocks outcome where rate hikes have little impact on growth or employment, while allowing inflation to gently glide towards targets over the next few years. As Figure 1 shows, there was little change in projections outside of lowering the UER, which was mostly a mark to market. Shockingly, growth was marked up despite the 50 bps increase in rates (including this hike), indicating that AI spend will continue to power growth , something Warsh touched upon in his presser. In turn, inflation readings for this year were modestly higher, another mark to market of higher energy prices , with minimal (but not non -existent) knock on into core readings. Overall forward inflation was left unchanged versus June’s SEP estimates, falling towards targets only after 2028. Finally, the long run estimate inched higher. This aligns with the idea that stronger growth can persist as strong capital demand is resilient despite rising interest rates, reflecting an environment where the neutral rate is shifting higher. Inflation remains overwhelmingly energy-driven: energy prices rose 15.5%Y and contributed just over 1ppt to headline inflation, while CPI excluding food and energy was 2.1%Y. • Core inflation remained contained. CPI-Median was unchanged at 2.0%Y and CPI-Trim held at 1.9%Y, with both measures still close to target. The data continue to show little evidence of broad second-round pass-through from higher energy prices. • Gasoline inflation has moved in line with global crude prices and fell sequentially in August. Brent prices have once again risen above $100/bbl, and gasoline inflation is likely to pick up again in September. Travel-related inflation accelerated on a 12-month basis, but this is largely a base-effect story rather than a fuel effect. • Food inflation continued to cool. Food inflation slowed to 2.9%Y from 3.1% in July and 3.4% in June, while grocery inflation eased to 2.8%. After remaining elevated for much of the past year, food is becoming a smaller source of inflation pressure. • Shelter remained subdued. The government is instead reportedly preparing relief measures on fuel prices, most likely through another temporary fuel tax cut, as in summer. This would ease acute cost-of-living pressures at limited fiscal cost. If announced this week, it should help reduce the risk of the coalition parties underperforming in Sunday’s state elections in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, helping to stabilize the government into the autumn. However, this would provide only temporary relief. The government’s more fundamental problem is that Germany’s nascent economic recovery has yet to deliver a political dividend. The AfD’s narrative of “de-industrialization” continues to resonate with widespread economic frustration. Although the recent surge in fuel prices is an acute concern, household surveys suggest that inflation expectations have remained stable this year, while fears of unemployment have increased. In our view, the continued decline in manufacturing employment is currently the most important driver of populist resentment. records.text: Euro Area: Rates Strategy Ain't no yield high enough After the multi-sigma shock of last week, EUR rates have found some support but energy prices remain firmly in the driving seat. We discuss long-end EGB ASW dynamics given the intensity of recent moves, and update our swap positioning indicators. Peak pain or more in train? Following the four-sigma shock last Thursday, the pain in EUR rates extended over the next two trading sessions before marginally softer oil and gas prices brought some stability. With key central bank meetings this week, the running question across client conversations has been how far the front-end can go given the purely supply-driven nature of the shock. After all, across key DM central banks, markets are pricing a further c.50-100bp of tightening over the next 12 months. A challenging admission highlighted in these conversations was that despite the cheap levels in EUR rates, the market remained entirely in the throes of energy price developments. Given the velocity of recent moves across various pockets of the market, things do look stretched but the question is one of conviction and the courage to fade the levels especially given the ECB's message last week. The ECB staff projections from last week show 2027 growth at trend (1.4%) despite being marked off a c.3% terminal rate, ie, the ECB forecast that even with policy rates c.100bp above the middle of its neutral rate zone, the euro area would still be able to grow at trend. Source: Citi Research, Refinitiv FX: Asymmetry favors EURCHF downside While we remain patient as FX trades to the macro backdrop, we like positioning for EURCHF downside as the French presidential election approaches. In thinking about the 2027 French presidential election, we ask ourselves: 1. When will this start to matter for EUR? 2. Where do we see the asymmetry? 3. What might the impact look like across scenarios? In identifying timing, we take two simple approaches. First, we examine inflection points around 5y French CDS – our preferred cross-asset signal – ahead of prior French presidential elections (Figure 1). Second, after controlling for rate differentials, we examine when the 10y OAT-Bund spread becomes a more ‘significant’ predictor of EURCHF in French election years. Both roughly suggest a window of ~ 2.5 months ahead of the first round, on average, which we treat as our benchmark. This would imply, all else equal, cross-asset indicators could begin reflecting such risk into February 2027. Interestingly, we already observe OATs screening cheap and French CDS grinding higher. But we expect FX will continue trading the broader macro backdrop for now (e.g. relative central bank dynamics, geopolitical risk), which invites patience when positioning for the French election in EUR. The unemployment rate has, so far, held steady below the Bank’s 5% forecast for Q3, although there are growing signs of slack, with more workers struggling to find new jobs quickly (Figure 4). This has kept the normalization in wage pressures largely intact, with private sector pay growth running notably below the BoE’s inflation target-consistent estimate of 3.25%. On the growth side, momentum has held up rather well considering the raft of headwinds facing the UK economy. Nevertheless, we would caution against reading too much into the headline, given that the strength in recent GDP prints has mostly been a one-man show. Services have been the dominant catalyst to the more positive growth story, masking the sluggish activity in more rate-sensitive sectors such as manufacturing and industrial production. This speaks to policy already being more restrictive than that in the US and Europe, reinforced by the fact that rates stand 75bps above the BoE’s neutral estimate range . Moreover, the lack of fiscal headroom and Chancellor Healey’s pledge of budget responsibility reduces the prospects of any meaningful fiscal stimulus in the near -term, adding to the restrictive backdrop. Overall, this pushes back against the notion that the BoE should hike simply to keep pace with its peers or risk falling behind. records.text: M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 25 Chemicals Lisa De Neve, Selina Wang Higher EU gas prices = earnings risk? Natural gas (and power) is a key energy source (to make steam and process heat) and feedstock (to chemically convert into a product such as ammonia) for our Industrial Chemical and Fertiliser coverage. A €10/MWh change in gas prices has an average unhedged impact of ~5% to EBITDA (we use 2026 EBITDA consensus as baseline) across our coverage, with Yara (~12%) > K+S (8%) > Solvay (~6%) > BASF (~4%) having the highest exposures. We note that various chemical players have material 'hedging' policies in place (i.e. having locked in the price of some of their energy consumption) including Solvay/K+S/BASF (~80%/~70%/specific % not disclosed, respectively, for FY26), and hence actual earnings risk from higher natural gas (and power) prices is much lower. On the other side, Yara does not hedge, but it's worth noting that Europe is currently the marginal supplier/buyer in the urea market, and hence urea prices may move higher as well (if not partially). Hence, we see less risk to FY26 earnings, potentially some could face higher energy costs in 4Q26 (e.g. there may be a LSD% earnings risk for K+S on 2H26), but there could be more material earnings risk for 1H27, especially for BASF/Solvay and to a lesser extent K+S, if the Morgan Stanley Commodities team's natural gas estimates of €85/MWh and €53/MWh for 1Q/2Q27 respectively materialise. We think that short-term narrative is clouding the more constructive medium-term outlook. Canada is entering a two-stage acceleration in growth that should be driven by productivity, which in turn should come from capital deepening and efficiency gains. With the investment pipeline that is currently in train, we think capital deepening can push potential growth up about 1/4pp from about 1½% to almost 1¼%. But we see scope for even more acceleration, with potential rising perhaps to 2% as the capital build broadens across the economy, and eventually, demographics should flip from a drag to a boost. The first stage of Canada’s acceleration is capital deepening, creating more capital per worker to start to raise productivity. That stage is likely to run through the end of the 2020s. The second stage is the 2030s, when demographics are likely to shift and the denominator in the capital-labor ratio should be on the rise again. Some of the first stage is already under way, and indeed some of it is arithmetic. As employment slows, capital-labor ratio can rise even without a dramatic acceleration in investment. In our view, that outcome improves the starting point but does not by itself establish a new growth regime. records.text: European Economic Comment14 September 2026 ab 2 What to expect from the inflation forecast As usual, the conditional inflation forecast should be viewed as the main guidance tool (for a detailed discussion see the focus article in our September 2025 Switzerland quarterly). The main elements to watch are the end-point in Q2 2029 and the slope of the forecast. We expect the SNB to revise up its oil price assumption, take into account the past weakening of the CHF and to assume further CHF weakness going forward based on the increased ECB-SNB rate differential. Against this backdrop, we expect the 2026 forecast to remain unchanged at 0.6% (the main impact of the revised assumptions will only be in Q4 2026), but lift 2027 by 30bp to 0.9% and 2028 by 10bp to 0.8%. For the Q2 2029 end-point, we expect 1% - a 0.2pp increase from the 0.8% the SNB projected last time. Overall, this forecast would signal that inflation still remains at low levels, but - given the upward slope - is expected to move in the right direction. If the end-point were to be revised to notably above 1%, we would consider this an explicitly hawkish policy signal, indicating an increased probability for earlier lift-off, possibly as soon as in the next meeting in December. We note that historically the SNB has tended to increase the policy rate when the end-point of its forecast was 1.75% or higher. This has also supported Europe, which has relatively less Tech exposure, although it faces other headwinds from higher gas prices and politics from here. We like a barbell strategy of a well-diversified portfolio of global AI-exposed stocks and high-dividend, low-volatility stocks. While low-volatility and high-dividend stocks have lagged the broad market since the COVID-19 crisis, they have performed better relative to the market excluding Tech (Exhibit 28). And in Tech-driven equity drawdowns, like the Deepseek sell-off in Q1 2025 and the momentum unwind in July 2026, they materially outperformed. In fact, the proportion of stocks with a negative beta to the market has increased sharply, very similar to the Tech Bubble (Exhibit 29). How relevant are CTAs as a market mover? To gauge how likely it is that changes in CTA positioning will contribute to spot moves, we have derived a ‘CTA Importance indicator’ which combines a measure of changes in CTA activity (the standard deviation of the changes in CTA weights) with a measure of trading volumes (the volume sub-component of the buy/sell pressure component in FX positioning). We think that when periods of high CTA activity correspond to periods of lower volumes, one can infer that CTAs are a greater proportion of total flows and therefore more likely to drive spot moves as their positioning changes. This would correspond to a higher value of the CTA importance indicator, which is expressed as a 5y percentile . The CTA importance indicator for EUR (Figure 3) currently sits at the 83rd percentile, the highest reached since mid-2024, indicating that CTAs are relatively more important for EURUSD than they have been in recent years. However, a key question is how it would perform under alternative macroeconomic scenarios. Based on recent equity price action, we observe that markets may be shifting how they price growth under higher inflation. For most of the summer, we have operated in the reflation quadrant, characterized by high global growth and high inflation. However, as geopolitical conflicts impact major oil producers like Saudi Arabia, there is a risk of a transition toward stagflation—meaning low growth and high inflation. How our portfolio would react to sustained stagflation is less clear and depends heavily on the reaction of energy markets. What we do know is that if we transition from reflation to stagflation and continue in that direction, the subsequent macroeconomic scenario is recession. In a recessionary environment, low growth becomes the dominant force, putting us in a quadrant of low growth and low inflation. This transition would pose the most significant short-term risk to Portfolio 365 if a rapid repricing occurs. A recessionary shock would imply falling energy prices and rising bond prices, which is the exact opposite of our current positioning. To be clear, in a recessionary shock, our defensive overlay would rally, but our pro-cyclical and balanced overlays would weaken and drag down the overall performance of Portfolio 365. Those constraints gave us an implicit timeline, and we expected that by June there would be some form of agreement to reopen the Strait. Based on current supply and demand conditions, we estimate September fair value at $90, yet Brent is trading at $106. records.text: Cayla Seder, Filippo Ferone 16 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material BOE Preview : Is the cart in front of the horse? Ahead of this week’s BoE meeting, markets have rapidly embraced a more hawkish outlook, moving from pricing less than one hike through year-end to fully pricing 100bps of tightening over the next nine months. We think that shift looks difficult to justify. While inflation risks remain elevated and may warrant further tightening over time, the BoE’s communication has remained broadly neutral . L abor market conditions continue to soften, and policy is already restrictive. As a result, we see current pricing as vulnerable to disappointment, particularly given the lack of support from central bank messaging or a meaningful improvement in the macro backdrop. With higher rate expectations failing to generate meaningful real money demand for Sterling, we remain cautious on GBP heading into the meeting. The difference a week can make . On September 8, OIS markets were pricing just 2bps of tightening for the BoE’s September meeting, 31bps by December, and 72bps by July 2027. Seven days later, market pricing has turned notably more hawkish. While the move for September remains modest, two hikes are nearly fully priced by December and four by Ju ne 2027. records.text: thly Payment at 7% Mortgage Rates Source: NAR, Freddie Mac, US Census Bureau, Morgan Stanley Research What have those prior periods of steep mortgage rate increases meant for sales? The answer is that it depends. In periods of time where the increase was brief, home sales tended to do well over the next year. When that increase was sustained over several months, sales were more likely to be flat-to-down. As always with the housing market, the direction of travel depends on myriad variables from inventory, to credit availability, affordability, and so much more than just mortgage rates. But coming back to affordability, just how far are we from returning to some sense of a normal affordability environment? The severity of the housing cycles over the past few decades has made it difficult to define what exactly a "normal" or "equilibrium" housing market is. In the chart below, we show what it would take in both mortgage rate terms and home price terms to bring affordability back to different longer-run averages (Exhibit 4 ).

records.text: M Idea 44 Energy Shell (SHEL LN) Martijn Rats, Alice Winograd Rating: Overweight; Price Target: GBp 3,780/sh (Upside to PT: 6%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: Shell has underperformed peers for most of the last year, but both factors behind that are now turning, underpinning our new Overweight rating. The first was resource longevity: Shell's longer-term production outlook has been amongst the weakest in the peer group, but the now-completed ARC Resources acquisition adds ~400 kb/d of existing production and holds the profile stable to 2032 on our analysis. The second is an ongoing policy of raising the dividend by 4% annually, which lags both Shell's financial capacity and its cash flow visibility. We believe management will move away from its preference for buybacks as the preferred "flex" on distributions, allowing for stronger dividend growth and a re-rating of shares. This reset may already have started, with a usual off-cycle 5% increase at 1Q26, which CFO Sinead Gorman tied to confidence in the long-term duration of Shell's cash flows. Broader idiosyncratic drivers. Shell's drivers are broadly unrelated to AI and are primarily tied to capital allocation. Valuation: On a "clean" FCF yield (after lease payments and hybrid bond coupons), Shell trades at 12-13% for 2026/27e, against ~10% for the average European integrated. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 14 Sep 2026 07:58:49 ET │ 10 pages US Economics FOMC Preview – One hike, not a cycle CITI'S TAKE The combination of slightly stronger than expected core CPI and the renewed rise in energy prices is likely just enough to push consensus toward hiking 25bp at this week’s meeting. The decision to hike could be unanimous, but we would not be surprised by up to two dissents in favor of a hold. The rate increase is likely to be presented as a “calibration” and not the start of a cycle of hikes. Core PCE inflation projections should be revised lower as officials take into account upcoming methodological revisions. With growing evidence that underlying inflation is slowing and that energy prices are not passing through to broad consumer prices, our base case is for the Fed to hike just once and then return to cuts in June 2027. records.text: The degree to which the US equity market is currently “expensive” depends in large part on the sustainability of recent earnings strength. The exceptional recent strength of earnings has driven an unusual wedge between equity valuation multiples based on near-term earnings and valuations on trend earnings. Because equity prices have failed to keep pace with surging earnings, near-term valuations show no hint of a bubble: The S&P 500 12-month P/E ratio has declined from 23x a year ago to 19x today and now matches its 10-year average. However, even an “average” multiple may be expensive if current earnings are unsustainable. The cyclically-adjusted P/E based on trailing 10-year earnings has climbed to one of its highest levels on record, falling shy of the highs of 1999-2000 but surpassing the level reached in 2021. Similarly, our colleagues have argued that the increase in market value of AI companies during the last few years requires an optimistic estimate of the future magnitude of AI-related profits and who will capture them. records.text: 2 Insights A big ask for the BoJ and a split decision from the BoE The Fed is not the only major central bank struggling to meet immediate and future tightening expectations this week. In our July BoJ preview, A crisis of cadence, we argued that its tightening cycle required more urgency. That has now arrived in a rush. At the end of July, the next move was not fully priced until December and the probability of a September hike was just over 25%. Today, hikes are fully priced for September, December and April next year. Inflation, wages and even the BoJ’s reported tone still support more frequent hikes, but exceeding these expectations will be difficult. We nevertheless retain a positive JPY view for six reasons. First, as Figure 2 shows, asset managers are aggressively buying back their JPY shorts. Rate markets may be fully priced for the new BoJ, but FX positions are not. For the rest, five of our six machine selections remain long JPY (page 4). This agreement across our machine learning processes led us to increase our long JPY exposure at the start of the month in Uncertainty and Contrarian JPY convictions, initially this was driven by a valuation concerns, but now momentum and holdings factors are contributing too. We retain our CHFJPY short even with BoJ expectations so high. Our long EURGBP idea also faces central bank risk this week. The ECB delivered its hike with some hawkish language, albeit from uncertain sources, while all BoE hikes are priced for after September

on of restrictive versus accommodative without the concept of a neutral rate. The chair could be using imprecise language – referring to broad financial conditions as opposed to the federal funds rate – but until we know more, we assume the language choice was intentional. Warsh’s reaction function is still incomplete, but it is clear it includes geopolitics and commodity-price transmission to inflation Warsh identified geopolitics as one of the three developments that changed between July, when the committee held steady, and September, when it raised rates. He said: “The third thing that has changed in seven weeks is geopolitics. There is no hiding from hot spots around the world, and our judgment about what is the most likely, or least likely, of the geopolitical situation has changed.” His concern also extends beyond the direct effect of energy prices on headline inflation. In discussing the factors driving the increase in long-term yields, Warsh cited geopolitics as a leading explanation and emphasized transmission through commodity-processing margins: “The third [reason behind higher interest rates] is geopolitics. The situation, hot spots around the world, are driving long-term yields. It is not simply spot prices of energy… but it is the difference between those spot prices and so-called crack spreads. What that means for products that find their way into a store across the country.”

records.text: Paul Gabard 17 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General SNB preview: Peak Dovishness? The SNB enters next week's meeting as the most dovish central bank in the G10 according to our MediaStats framework, yet markets continue to price around two hikes across the next four meetings. We expect the SNB to leave rates unchanged at 0.00% and maintain a balanced message. While August CPI rose to 0.8% YoY from 0.4%, inflation remains within the SNB's 0-2% price stability range and core CPI is only 0.4% YoY. Chairman Martin Schlegel has repeatedly emphasized that Switzerland's inflation pickup is smaller than elsewhere and that the SNB does not see second-round effects. While we struggle to justify the 2+ hikes over the next four meetings that were priced by the markets earlier today, we also believe the hurdle for a renewed dovish shift has risen materially. The key tension going into next week's meeting is between market pricing and the SNB's own narrative. Markets currently price around 33% of a hike by year-end and around two hikes over twelve months. However, our MediaStats hawkish-dovish indicators continues to rank the SNB as the most dovish central bank in the G10 (Figure 1). The August inflation data provide some justification for reducing downside policy expectations, but for now, not enough to warrant the degree of tightening embedded in Swiss rate markets over the next year, in our view. records.text: ates a negative demand and cost squeeze across the automotive ecosystem, delaying recovery and reinforcing cyclical weakness. Investors still find relative safety in tyres. Tyre manufacturers tend to offer relative defensiveness within the automotive value chain, which also appears to be often true during energy price spikes. Structurally, tyres benefit from a high exposure to replacement demand (typically ~75%), with only ~25% linked to original equipment (OE), meaning that even during economic downturns, when new vehicle sales weaken, drivers still need to maintain existing vehicles, supporting a more resilient demand profile. This does not make tyre volumes immune to declines, but it does make them less cyclical than OEMs and suppliers. Consistent with this, we note that tyres have been the best-performing segment in three of the historical periods of energy price spikes in our analysis, highlighting their relative safe-haven characteristics within autos. The notable exception is the Russia/ Ukraine conflict, where tyres underperformed the most; however, we think this could be an outlier, driven by tyre-specific supply chain disruptions and a comparatively stronger operating backdrop for OEMs and suppliers at the time. By contrast, suppliers tend to be the worst performers across these periods, reflecting their typically weaker balance sheets, higher operating leverage, and greater exposure to cyclical production volumes, all of which make them higher beta stocks. The recovery remains narrow with the earnings growth of the remaining sectors (ex-tech, upstream and financials) down 8% in 1H26. Consumption exposed sectors remained under pressure with consumer sector earnings contracting for the fifth consecutive quarter while autos also reported a 19% earnings decline despite robust export orders. For the internet sector, while competitive intensity in food delivery has started to ease, increased AI-related investment has weighed on profitability as meaningful monetization takes time to materialize. Meanwhile, we noted SG&A expenses increased across a number of sectors as companies stepped up spending on marketing amid intensifying domestic competition (Figure 32). The Bank cares incredibly about the domestically generated components of inflation. Core CPI has been slowing toward the Bank’s target, averaging around 2.3% since April. While services inflation is still well above 3%, it has been on a gradual downward trend since summer of 2023, reflecting in part the gentle easing in wages and labour market pressure over the last three years. The degree of services inflation stickiness is something the Bank watches closely, and factors into their judgements. Policy options Current market pricing anticipates around four hikes from the Bank of England by next summer. We think this is excessive, not least given the Bank’s remarkable degree of tolerance for headline CPI being above target over the last five years. However, given the size of the inflation problem, alongside the recent improvement in growth some policy tightening is necessary and likely. Given energy prices, one might be tempted to assume the UK is now in something akin to the Bank’s ‘Adverse’ scenario from July. But we think that the similarities are superficial. Using our rule of thumb that every 1 mbd of supply disruption adds roughly $4 to the price, that $16 premium implies the market is pricing in the risk of an additional 4 mbd of losses on top of the 10 mbd already disrupted—rather than a confirmed, enduring reduction in supply. And there is no shortage of risk for the market to price. Over the past week, the conflict has opened new pressure points across the region. Houthi advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and into the Bab el-Mandeb have put another critical shipping route at risk, while an attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline temporarily shut a key alternative route for crude exports. Nor is the volatility contained to the Gulf. Despite President Trump’s claim of an energy truce, Ukrainian drones struck Russia’s Slavyansk refinery on Saturday and, in a more significant display of reach, hit the Taneco refinery in Tatarstan— more than 1,200 km from the Ukraine-Russia border—on Sunday, followed by the Syzran refinery in Russia’s Samara region on Monday. Meanwhile, Russia launched attacks on the Ukrainian capital and other cities. records.text: UK Real Estate Paul May, CFA Barclays, UK | Kanad Mitra Barclays, UK What makes UK real estate assets attractive today? UK Real Estate offers contractually backed income, moderating new supply (higher financing and construction costs are restricting development) and, critically, structurally lower listed- market cost of capital versus stressed private owners. Private equity holders face 12-15%+ return hurdles that existing portfolios cannot clear, while fund maturities and LP redemption pressure are forcing disposals – creating a rare buyers' market for well-capitalised listed vehicles. This is not a new phenomenon. We first flagged the "buy the buyers" opportunity in December 2023, developed it through 2024 (Buy the Buyers and Buy British, July 2024; Buy the buyers, 4 Oct 2024), and have watched it play out in the UK in real time: Tritax Big Box's acquisition of UKCM (2024) and a £1bn+ Blackstone portfolio, LondonMetric's takeouts of LXi REIT , Urban Logistics and Highcroft (growing its portfolio from £3.0bn to £7.6bn since 2023), PHP's merger with Assura, British Land's purchase of Life Science REIT , and now Prologis's £14.3bn agreed takeover of SEGRO. records.text: The AI boom and S&P 500 earnings growth Affirming investor concerns that US companies are “over-earning,” there are three factors that are boosting earnings today but will contribute to deceleration going forward: 1) AI capex spending, 2) semiconductor margin expansion, and 3) earnings from private investment gains. AI capex The AI investment boom is driving nearly half of S&P 500 EPS growth this year, but its contribution will fade going forward. The mega-cap US hyperscalers are on track to spend $800 billion on capex this year, an increase of 94% vs. 2025. That spending is flowing through to the earnings of the AI infrastructure complex including semiconductor, tech hardware, industrials, and utilities companies, which are collectively accounting for roughly half of consensus S&P 500 earnings growth this year. The AI boom is also having a secondary impact on earnings outside of the infrastructure complex, for example by boosting capital markets activity and consumer wealth. Both consensus and GS analyst forecasts show hyperscaler capex growing at a slower rate in coming years, which should result in decelerating earnings growth for much of the AI infrastructure complex and a fading tailwind to S&P 500 earnings.
