records.text: ch an environment, if inflation is rising, central bank raises policy rates causing bond yields to rise as both average short-term rates and inflation risk premium move higher. Bond and stock returns go lower together. This was the situation from 1965 to 1980. If inflation is falling, the reverse is true with yields declining (positive bond returns) and positive equity returns (from 1981 to 1995). The average 60-day correlation between bond and stock returns over the period 1965-1995 was +0.29 (Figure 2E q u i t y - B o n d C o r r e l a t i o n ). If inflation expectations are well anchored, inflation will fluctuate around the anchor depending on growth. Higher growth (higher stock returns) will be associated with higher inflation, higher yield and lower bond returns. Conversely, when growth weakens (stock returns fall), inflation also decreases and bond returns are higher, i.e. negative correlation of bond and stock returns. This was broadly the case from 1996 to 2021, with average 60-day correlation of -0.24. Since then, inflation expectations seem shakier and term structure of breakeven rates suggests that inflation expectations are anchored closer to 2.5% rather than the Fed’s target of 2.0%. The average 60-day stock-bond correlation from 2022 to now is slightly positive at +0.09, higher than pre-Covid level but much lower than the 1965-1995 average. However, the Committee's tone has clearly turned more hawkish. First, the MPC noted that upside risks to the inflation outlook have increased since July. Second, it noted that spot energy prices were close to the July adverse scenario (although futures curves remain lower), which assumed tighter policy to bring inflation back to target. Third, the Committee emphasised that the risk of material second-round effects had increased since July. This view was shared by the six MPC members who voted to keep rates unchanged. In this context, the MPC emphasised that, "[g]iven the lags with which second-round effects appeared, it was not appropriate to wait too long for evidence of such effects before responding with policy." Governor Bailey, previously seen as an important swing voter, was even more explicit in his individual paragraph, stating that the policy stance might need to tighten "if the conflict in the Middle East persists for an extended period, as appears to be the case, and the risk of second-round effects emerging increases." In the very near term energy prices and central bank policy will likely drive both bonds and equities – rates relief would support both but continued increases in yields could weigh more on equities. However, over the next few months, resilient earnings growth should continue to support risk-adjusted returns for equities vs. bonds. That said, over longer horizons, higher starting yields should lift optimal bond allocations from the unusually low levels of the past five years towards historical norms. There is unlikely to be an immediate return to the simple 60/40 portfolio n template. Investors should favour the parts of the curve with the best carry vs. convexity – with relatively low rates volatility, selective option overlays can help. We also like bond-like equities to improve diversification with a growing number of stocks with a negative beta. On the flip side, equity-like bonds such as convertibles look more attractive to improve asymmetry. Polling shows a consistent lead for Freitas, with the September Quaest poll placing him at 42% of first-round voting intentions compared with Haddad’s 27%. When cash returns are higher, cash can dominate bonds, making it optimal for investors to pair equities with cash according to their risk tolerance, as has been the case over the past 5 years. This shift is closely tied to equity/bond correlations: when correlations are positive, bonds tend to offer less diversification benefit; when they are negative, required bond returns tend to fall below cash returns due to the additional diversification value bonds provide. Returns on cash relative to bonds have varied materially since 1900 – in the last 5 years long-dated bonds have underperformed cash materially (Exhibit 18). In the 1910s and the 1960-80s and post the COVID-19 crisis bonds underperformed cash for prolonged periods, which boosted the optimal equity weight. On the flip side, for the previous generation of investors, up until the COVID-19 crisis, bonds generally outperformed vs. cash, and with negative equity/bond correlations since the late 1990s there has generally been a case for higher bond allocations. Bond markets have started to adjust to the new macro and monetary policy regime with higher neutral rates and steeper global yield curves. US 5y5y forward real yields are near their average since 1960, suggesting markets are already pricing a higher ‘neutral rate’ equilibrium (Exhibit 19). records.text: While we expect inflation to normalise into 2027, which should support more negative equity/bond correlations, bonds may offer less protection than they have over the past 30 years. At the start of S&P 500 bear markets since 1950, the median nominal yield was about 4.7%, real yields were 2.3%, and breakeven inflation was around 2.5% (Exhibit 17). Both after the Tech Bubble burst and during the GFC, US 10-year yields fell by c.200bp. Current US 10-year yields are still below Tech Bubble peaks, implying a smaller potential buffer. And while yields during the GFC were similar to current levels, breakeven inflation then fell sharply on deflation fears. Higher nominal growth could limit declines in long-dated yields in the next recession, unless the growth or inflation outlook deteriorates materially. The next crisis may also involve more fiscal spending and less central bank QE, limiting potential bond yield declines. UK Capital Goods Jonathan Hurn, CFA Barclays, UK What makes assets in your sector attractive today? UK Capital Goods combines high-quality assets with undemanding valuations, a factor underpinning the sector's rising corporate activity trend. The sector comprises end-market leaders with strong profitability (sector average EBITA margin of c17%) and low leverage (net debt/EBITDA of c1x). Average market cap across UK Cap Goods is c£5bn, making these genuinely midcap, digestible targets for both financial (PE) and strategic/trade acquirers, as well as activist shareholders seeking to unlock value not reflected in current share prices. Historically, periods of elevated M&A activity have coincided with widened gaps between public market pricing and intrinsic/SOTP value. Recent transactions are consistent with this pattern: e.g., Spectris was acquired by KKR (completed 4Q25) and Bodycote received a recommended cash offer from Veritas (3Q26). These transactions confirm PE and trade buyers see value the public market does not, with more activity likely given how many names still trade below their SOTP . In terms of the energy mix, this differs by business type. A Fed hiking cycle may eventually help, but the near-term test for funding markets is whether money funds can absorb growing bill supply without a broader repricing in front-end rates. One theme we have been tracking over the past few weeks is the tepid pace of inflows into money market funds. We recently highlighted this trend (see here), but with the Fed delivering a 25bp hike this week, one question has become more pressing: will higher rates be enough to bring cash back into money funds? It is an important issue for funding markets because money funds remain the dominant buyers of Treasury bills just as bill issuance is set to pick up in Q4. To put some numbers on the slowdown in inflows, over the same period last year, money fund AUM increased by roughly $450bn, compared with about $200bn so far this year ( Figure 1). That compares with annual inflows over the past few years of roughly $800bn to more than $1trn. In short, money fund balances have grown more slowly than investors have become accustomed to, raising questions about who will absorb the next wave of Treasury bill supply. The reason for this, we would assume, is to provide certainty for the total QT envelope while it conducts active QT. Nor will it sell Gilts maturing beyond 2049, which will be retained to maturity. They, the Bank says, will be backing the stock of banknotes, rendering seigniorage more explicit to an extent. We suspect the fact that the very longest Gilts trade at the largest discount to their original purchase cost might also be a factor. The important thing to stress is that the net value of Gilts to be absorbed by the market from active sales will be the same. We will get an extra £20bn Gilt sales from the DMO rather than £20bn from the Bank. (Strictly speaking it would not have been £20bn from the Bank, it would have been perhaps £14bn in sale proceeds plus £6bn paid by the Treasury under the indemnity to cover crystalised losses). The smallest cycle so far was the 137.5bps increase across the four hikes in 1986-87. Every cycle is different and this may end up being a baby cycle by historical standards. That said, it is rare for a hiking cycle not to bring higher yields over the following year. If you're looking for some offset to that, the average move for 10yr USTs is +114bps over that period despite most historical cycles being considerably more aggressive than this one is expected to be. So it’s not usually a positive for rates when the Fed hikes but there are some reasons why this cycle might be better than many others for yields. The most important performance dynamic for us post the first hike is related to quality, which outperforms in every window into and out of the first hike ( Exhibit 7 ). This all makes sense in the context of our early-to-mid-cycle transition call, where the market is now placing greater emphasis on earnings durability, margin stability, free cash flow and operational efficiency—supportive of both our quality bias and the S&P 500 at the index level given its significant quality weight. The changing dynamic at the Fed this spring was an important driver of our call and last week's data reinforces it. Bottom line, we would use any near-term volatility around the first hike to remain anchored in quality (see here for our screen). The risks are not a 25 basis point hike in September in and of itself; they are: a rapid rise in oil prices from here as the Strait remains closed, China coming back into the oil market and/or diesel crack spreads narrowing from rising oil, rather than falling diesel prices. This energy-related outcome or broader inflation pressure than what we've seen would likely influence back-end yields and the expected terminal rate in a manner that would be accompanied by higher bond volatility. records.text: sequence of hikes. The projections suggest that for the policy rate to move materially above the median path, inflation would likely need to reaccelerate and the labor market tighten more than expected. We do not think that stronger growth in Q3 by itself is likely to produce those outcomes. In other words, the most likely path of policy rates is the one that is now being projected by the FOMC’s dots; in contrast, the market's most likely expected path of policy rates involves nearly three more hikes. The ECB raised the deposit rate to 2.50% last week, and our economists expect another 25bp hike in December, with risks skewed towards further tightening if the energy outlook deteriorates. However, underlying inflation declined in August, wages have not responded materially to the energy shock and longer-term inflation expectations remain close to 2%. The economy in Europe too has managed to be more resilient to the price shock than was anticipated. The BoE’s decision is also informative. The MPC voted 6-3 to keep Bank Rate at 3.75%, despite a further rise in the near-term inflation forecast and greater upside risks. This divergence is visible globally, but especially in the US. There are several reasons for this divergence. Cross-country relationships n confirm that high price levels are lowering sentiment, while amplified political biases have led to sharp shifts after recent global elections that brought change in political leadership. But the weakness in sentiment is also quite broad. Sentiment remains below 2019 levels for all groups in the US even after stratifying by wealth, income, generation, social media use, political party, and homeownership. One explanation for these patterns is that people have generally become more n downbeat on the state of the world for reasons unrelated to the economy. Consistent with this explanation, overall happiness levels deteriorated sharply in 2020 and have yet to recover, despite people’s assessment of their financial situation only deteriorating modestly. The median beta of EXD fund returns to EXD spreads The hypothesis: Rising betas portend spread widening This component measures how strongly the dedicated EM external debt fund universe is loading on broad EM credit beta. In conceptual terms, it asks whether the typical fund in the complex is behaving like a high-beta EM risk position, with spread performance increasingly driving returns. When that beta rises, it usually indicates that positioning has become more directional and more exposed to common market risk. Empirically, a higher median fund beta is associated with wider 4 week-ahead EM spreads. records.text: M Idea 2 EA Growth: Cautiously Optimistic Our View in a Nutshell What to make of strong 2Q26 EA GDP growth? The most recent estimate of 2Q26 Euro area GDP growth now stands at a quarterly pace of 0.6%Q (Exhibit 1 ) and 1.2%Y year-on- year ( Exhibit 2 ). Of course, this strong quarterly figure is lifted by Ireland printing at 10.2%Q. But 2Q26 growth in the EA excluding Ireland was also solid, at 0.3%Q, and ultimately a significant beat vs expectations (MSe: 0.15%Q, ECB June: 0.2%Q). Interestingly the robustness was broad-based across countries (except France). Our own estimate of the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) is more conservative, at 4.2% of GDP in 2026 and 2027, than the Ministry of Finance’s 4.1% and 3.9%. ▪ The consolidation rests almost entirely on revenue. The proposed changes to the corporate income tax base are a step forward, though we expect them to yiel d a permanent gain of around 0.3pp of GDP rather than the 0.7pp the Ministry anticipates . Expenditure holds at 26. 7% of GDP in 2027 and inflexible spending accounts for over 80% of the total. ▪ We expect the net debt ratio to reach 55% of GDP by the end of 2027. With the nominal interest rate on public debt above nominal GDP growth for a fourth consecutive year, we estimate that a primary balance of 1.1% of GDP would be required to stabilise the ratio, against the 0.5% programmed. We believe the Mexican government is falling short of its debt consolidation commitment , as we have argued in Latin America: Politics in the economic driving seat , dated 28 August . records.text: In the near-term, we estimate that the annualised pace of sales was only adding around 0.5ppts/GDP of 10y-equivalent free float to the market. As sales are now paused, the impact from this alone would be small, less than 1bp on swap spreads. However, with sales now operating through the DMO, the maturity transformation of future sales may have a bigger effect. Looking out to 2034, the average WAM of bonds to be sold is around 15 years currently (which will age over the 7 years of planned asset sales) (Exhibit 3). But if the DMO issue shorter maturity bonds, say at the WAM of current issuance over the last six months of 7 years, this would result in an effective reduction in the 10y-equivalent free-float of 3ppts of GDP , which would be worth more like 3bp on swap spreads. Finally, the cessation of long-end bond sales could contribute an even bigger impact on swap spreads, beyond the combined 4bp from our estimates, and beyond the 2bp move already priced in 30y Gilts vs OIS today. Despite the Gilt-positive news on active sales, the BoE’s plan signals a long horizon for QT. The net reduction in Gilt holdings of £46bn until 2034 was higher than the market expected, at least via the latest BoE dealer survey. This is likely to lead to greater Short-Term Repo (STR) facility use over time given that reserves look to be stabilising even as Gilt holdings continue to drop (Exhibit 4). Ironically indeed, despite stark ideological differences in many aspects, we argue the fiscal trajectory could end up looking quite similar under both RN or centrist leadership. In the case of a hung parliament, the case for the similarities is more straight-forward: only budgets sufficiently inoffensive to the major parties’ sensibilities can pass, as was the case in recent years. Budget deficits would be trimmed at the margins at best, only slowly moving from a 5% of GDP deficit to something closer to a 4% one over successive budget rounds. It would also very plausibly see a perpetuation of ‘temporary’ revenue measures, including corporate and high-income taxation. It’s not obvious that either side would embark on fiscal consolidation at pace. Even in the case of Presidential office and lower house under control by the same party or political bloc, a fiscal trajectory that would boost investor confidence is far from an assured outcome. Both the RN and centrists of course pledge to address fiscal profligacy, as high debt levels have started to unsettle not only markets, but also voters. records.text: 14 September 2026 Quant Snaps Deutsche Bank AG Page 3 [02:51] Portfolio 365 Performance and Strategy Exposure [Caio]: How is the quant world reacting to these developments? At the risk of sounding repetitive, our Portfolio 365 continues to perform well. It was up 70 basis points last week, with positive contributions coming from both the balanced and defensive overlays. The portfolio is up 1.4% for the month and close to 13% for the year, while maintaining a negative correlation to both equities and bonds. What is driving this month's performance? A significant driver remains its exposure to energy markets, a theme we have highlighted recently. Strategies such as commodity carry, commodity trend, and FX value are all performing strongly on the back of the energy rally. Our rates strategies, specifically momentum and long volatility, have also benefited—albeit more indirectly—through hawkish central bank activity. Meanwhile, the remainder of the portfolio—comprising roughly fifteen other strategies—has remained quiet. Our equity strategies are not highly correlated to energy, focusing instead on the AI theme, while our short volatility strategies have suffered slightly, as would be expected in this environment. Catalyst.Metric: AI-related tech exports contribution to real GDP growth

records.text: Capital spending on the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout continues to grow n rapidly. The majority of that spending goes to equipment manufactured in Asia. Consequently, our estimates for the contribution of tech exports to GDP in key n Asian producers continue to rise. For 2026, we estimate exports will provide a 7pp boost to real GDP growth in Taiwan, and 2-3pp in Korea, Vietnam, and Malaysia, with Singapore close behind. Beyond exports, we see increasing evidence of a lift to capital spending in Asia—n both in terms of productive capacity for exports, and in local data center investment. Consumption is likely benefiting on the margin from positive equity wealth effects in several economies. And in Korea and Taiwan, surging corporate tax receipts are supporting faster growth in government spending. However, the overall AI-related boost to domestic demand remains small in comparison to the export impact — well under 1pp of GDP ex-Taiwan. The European steel debate is shifting to whether mills can pass through a renewed rise in input costs. TTF prices have climbed ~80% since early July to ~€80/MWh, the highest since early 2023, as supply disruptions and sub-seasonal storage tighten the winter balance. Looking at bellwether ArcelorMittal, we estimate each €10/MWh increase removes ~US$8/t of EBITDA before hedging and mitigation, or US$200-250mn across ~30mt of European shipments. The move since 1 July therefore implies a gross annualised headwind of ~US$0.8bn. Premium HCC (coking coal) has also risen by ~US$50/t versus the 2Q average, adding ~US$25/t to blast-furnace steel production costs and taking the combined gas-and-coal cost increase to ~US$50-55/t ( Exhibit 29 ). For context, this represents ~5-6% of ArcelorMittal Europe’s ~US$1,000/t operating cost base. records.text: We have argued that interest rates have been rising this year mainly because of stronger nominal GDP growth (Exhibit 1 ) rather than heightened concern about the US Treasury's ability to fund the government. While the latter should not be ignored, we think the evidence is straightforward, as discussed in our Weekly Warm-Up a few weeks ago and evidenced by a term premium that appears quite contained in the face of the recent focus on this debate (Exhibit 2 ). As a reminder, nominal GDP is running close to 7% on a five-year trailing average. It's also reaccelerated on an annual basis this year thanks to the OBBBA's capex incentives, the seemingly insatiable demand for compute, and the race to win the AI race with China. As we have long argued, equities can tolerate stickier back-end yields if they are driven largely by stronger nominal growth. In other words, equities remain a valuable inflation hedge over the intermediate-term. This also explains why the equity risk premium is close to zero for high quality stocks—i.e., the S&P 500. In short, equity investors should be careful what they wish for—deflation is the ultimate kryptonite for stocks, not inflation. If inflation were to get "out of control" and spike higher due to a new shock—i.e., oil prices making new highs—that is a different story. The current valuation discount is reflective of an erosion in returns from an c 19% long-term average ROIC to 6% (based on Barc 2027E). Methodology We calculate correlations between seasonally adjusted (SA) monthly changes in select CPI categories and PPI categories. The analysis includes detailed commodity PPI categories and final demand-intermediate demand (FD-ID) aggregates; commodity PPIs are the natural starting point because they classify prices by what is sold and therefore generally map more closely than industry PPIs to CPI categories. Restricting the study to SA series on both sides prevents recurring calendar patterns from driving the results. Results The accompanying heatmap shows the 30 strongest positive contemporaneous correlations among currently published, SA PPI and SA CPI categories with at least 96 overlapping months of data. It excludes energy and broad aggregates because those relationships are already well understood and tend to reflect mechanical or economy-wide inflation movements, rather than specific category links. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 13 Our economists currently expect one further ECB hike this cycle and note that additional tightening could become appropriate if gas prices remain elevated. A rise in TTF toward our €85/MWh forecast (or potentially our €100/MWh bull case) could therefore put further upward pressure on ECB pricing. There are good reasons why markets have so far focused on the ECB response rather than the growth cost of higher energy prices. Europe avoided recession in 2022 despite much higher gas prices (see our discussion here and our economists' discussion here); market pricing suggests subdued concerns about ECB-overtightening (see our discussion here and Exhibit 13 ); European corporates are less energy-intensive than they were in 2022 and better prepared for another energy shock; and global growth has remained relatively resilient (see the resilience of global labor markets in Exhibit 14 ). Together, those factors have reduced the perceived growth sensitivity of the Euro Area to higher energy prices and allowed the relative policy-rate channel to dominate. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 29 Capital Goods Legrand (LR FP) Max Yates, Sara Chemello Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €160/sh (Upside to PT: 13%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: Legrand has de-rated by ~20% year to date versus Electrical peers such as ABB and Schneider, driven by 1) concerns around Legrand's future data centre revenue growth in the context of their portfolio exposure to new 800v data centre architectures and 2) concerns following 1H26, where EBIT margins declined slightly while other Electrification names like Schneider and ABB saw margin expansion. We see these concerns as overdone and see an attractive entry point, with potential for three areas to surprise into 2027. 1) The fundamental reason to own Legrand is because, like other Electrical equipment companies, 2027 consensus estimates need to rise (our 2027 EBITA forecast is +6% vs consensus). The bull case on these stocks is that organic revenue growth estimates are too low for 2027, but the clear risk is that there likely has been some over-ordering in 2026, which may need to see some normalisation into 2027. We see Legrand as the best of both worlds. We see upside to 2027 organic growth estimates of 7.8%, and they do not disclose details on orders so there is less risk of disappointment around this element. We would be surprised if the SNB was giving indications in this regard and think it will rather stress that today's situation is different from 2022/23 when the SNB faced too high inflation and was preferring CHF strength. Recent client conversations showed mixed views about the SNB outlook: While Swiss investors on balance were expecting policy rates to remain on hold for a prolonged period, discussions with international investors focussed more on the risks of earlier, and potentially more, SNB hikes. Recap: SNB message in June was for unchanged rates The SNB kept rates on hold in June with the overall message broadly unchanged from March. It reiterated its "increased willingness" to intervene in FX markets (language introduced in March in the context of the Middle East tensions), albeit slightly modified by "if necessary". A weaker CHF has eased monetary conditions since then (the effective CHF has depreciated by c.2.5% since the June meeting) and reduced the need for actual purchases. records.text: The recent strength of S&P 500 earnings growth has raised investor concerns that the market is in an “earnings bubble.” S&P 500 EPS grew by 51% in Q2 and by 26% during the past four quarters, lifting earnings well above both the long-term trend and the historical relationship with economic growth. The S&P 500 forward P/E multiple sits at 19x, in line with its 10-year average, but the market multiple on trend earnings has only been exceeded in the past several decades during the peak of the Dot-Com Bubble. While there are indeed factors contributing to “over-earning” today, our base case is for S&P 500 earnings growth to decelerate, not collapse, in coming years. We forecast EPS growth of 11% in both 2027 (to $415) and 2028 ($460), driven by solid GDP growth and a fading tailwind from AI investment that gradually transitions into a growing boost from AI productivity. Energy prices and interest rates create near-term macro risks around these forecasts, but the impact of AI is the biggest long-term question for corporate earnings. The AI investment boom has accounted for nearly half of S&P 500 earnings growth this year, and this tailwind should begin to fade next year even as capex spending continues to grow. We estimate AI investment will transition from an S&P 500 earnings tailwind of 11 pp this year to a marginal drag in 2028 as capex growth slows and depreciation expenses mount. AI capex has repeatedly exceeded estimates during the last few years, and we outline upside and downside scenarios and their impact on S&P 500 profits. The recent surge in semiconductor profit margins also leaves S&P 500 earnings vulnerable to a decline in chip prices. Our industry analysts expect supply to remain tight through 2027 but for the rate of margin expansion to slow next year. An adverse scenario where semiconductor gross margins decline from 70% today to their 15-year average of 55% would cut S&P 500 earnings by roughly 10%. Appreciating equity stakes are also temporarily inflating S&P 500 earnings. The mega-cap tech companies generated over $150 billion of “other income” related to equity investments in Q2 2026, lifting S&P 500 earnings by 12%. We expect additional “other income” in H2 2026, but these accounting earnings should diminish in 2027. Excluding this income from 2026, our 2027 EPS forecast would reflect growth of 18%. Market pricing embeds an outlook for continued earnings growth but healthy skepticism regarding the sustainability of current profitability. records.text: Global Rates Markets Summary of views A summary of our views on duration, the curve, swap spreads, inflation, and volatility across the US, Europe, and Japan. United States Duration • 10y yields within striking distance of 5% reflect the markets having reassessed the expected• path higher while term premium appropriately hovers near pre-GFC levels. We remain of the view that bonds are not cheap yet. • The FOMC meeting outcome points to a modest recalibration of the policy stance to a more• resilient economy, rather than a hawkish shift in the reaction function, and does not create a long duration impulse. • We are neutral on duration.• Curve/curvature • We recommend 1yf 2s10s SOFR curve steepeners (entry -3bp), which can benefit from either• an inflation miss or the economy shrugging off hikes. • We maintain our recommendation to pay the belly of the 5s10s30s SOFR fly (1:2:1), as• Treasury's long-end purchases should reallocate term premium into the 10y sector, which looks too rich in light of the level of term premium. M&A in the airline industry has typically focussed on industry consolidation with airlines buying one another in pursuit of economies of scale or revenue synergies through economies of scope, strengthened market share or to secure scarce assets such as slots, traffic rights, aircraft or crew. For this reason consolidation is subject to strict competition policy scrutiny. Complex ownership and control rules in the airline industry also constrain cross-border consolidation, as well as investment by financial investors. We see the relevance of ownership and control restrictions fading in Europe and the UK does not apply ownership and control restrictions on UK airlines post Brexit. Yet this area is complex and there is an evident gap the in EU between current rules and the reality in the industry, as Ryanair’s low share (ca 30%) of EU ownership illustrates, contrary to the rules that require majority EU ownership and control for EU airlines. M&A involving financial investors taking listed airlines private is rarer but not unheard of: in 2019, the private equity group Onex took Canada’s second largest airline Westjet private. records.text: Bank into action this month. In previous BoE previews, we explained why we thought the Bank would keep rates unchanged this month. The story is the same: emerging labour market slack is a concern and nominal aggregates are still subdued. The 3m-on-3m measure of core CPI was most recently 1.7% and 2% in June and July respectively. Of course, monetary policy is about forward-looking inflation, and hence why the Bank went to incredible lengths in its last report to outline the process by which they will monitor emerging inflationary pressures. The MPC says it is concerned about second round effects – and it is – but the evidence thus far is limited, so any action to curb these could come with a delay. As we argued in advance of the July MPR, MPC members are weighing the tradeoffs. The division of opinion between the doves and hawks is due to two entirely different reaction functions. On the one hand, the doves view a holding position as restrictive given their assessment of the current stance of policy. On the other hand, the hawks care more about risk management and are concerned that the Bank’s credibility is eroding. One powerful argument on the doves’ side was the signal the Governor sent at his last press conference – that the BoE was not ‘edging towards a hike’ . It was an unusually clear and unambiguous statement. Overturning that by hiking in September would damage the ability of the Bank to make such statements in the future and have them be taken seriously by markets.

Rates price this with ~85% likelihood, up from just 35% likelihood just 2 weeks ago. The sharp shift in Fed pricing was catalyzed by Warsh Jackson Hole (JH) speech + stronger labor & inflation data. It is the first part of a previously very out-of-consensus 75bps hike in ’26 call from BofA US Economics. Fed faces simple choice at Sept FOMC: hike or risk large bond spike. If the Fed does not hike with current pricing, it risks a sharp and disorderly UST long end move. US 30Y could rapidly test 5.75%; UST buybacks would be futile to stop it. Bond price action, including post Friday’s CPI, shows the bond likes orthodoxy (Exhibit 2). Orthodoxy = use rate hikes to slow inflation & quell long end rate spike (not buybacks). Sept FOMC communications likely lean hawkish. SEP will show 50bps of total hikes in ’26, Waller may dovish dissent. Big Q: which Warsh in presser? July FOMC or JH Warsh? We think JH, largely to support bond. If right, UST curve likely to twist flatten, USD to be supported, & risk challenged. If wrong, bigger Bessent “house” needed for bond. records.text: “Other income” from private investment gains Appreciating equity investment stakes are also temporarily inflating S&P 500 earnings. In Q2 2026, the mega-cap tech companies enjoyed unrealized investment gains in private companies that totaled roughly $150 billion, translating into 12% of S&P 500 EPS. We expect H2 2026 reports will include additional “other income” that should be larger than the gains in Q1 but smaller than Q2 totals. We expect a much smaller contribution in 2027. The complete removal of this “other income” next year would create a drag of 8 pp on S&P 500 earnings growth in 2027 relative to 2026, all else equal. The fiscal trajectory is less ambitious than the one presented in April. The Ministry now targets a PSBR of 3.9% of GDP in 202 7, from 3.5% in the Preliminary General Criteria, which brings it closer to our estimates in Mexico: Incomplete fiscal consolidation , dated 9 April. We read the revision as recognition that the earlier path was not attainable on the expenditure side , rather than a change in the consolidation objective. The risks associated with these assumptions are tilted to the downside. Every additional dollar above the budgeted blend oil price yields the ministry MXN9.6bn (0.02% of GDP), so according to its own sensitivity estimates , a blend price maintained at current levels would generate excess oil revenues of up to MXN288bn (0.7% of GDP). This is a gross figure : the government has indicated the fuel excise stimulus would remain if international prices rose, which is likely to absorb part of the gain through lower excise collection, at a time when the Budget assumes excise revenues growing 10.5% in real terms. records.text: Dwyfor Evans 16 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General T urkey : Supported by Carry, Challenged by Easing The Turkish lira (TRY) has remained one of the more resilient high-carry currencies in the EM universe. Tight monetary policy, improving macro stability, reserve rebuilding, and a recovery in foreign investor participation have helped contain volatility and support confidence in Turkish assets. While we remain constructive on the TRY, the next phas e of the story may prove more challenging. As inflation continues to moderate and the prospect of CBRT rate cuts moves closer, investors will increasingly test the durability of Turkey's disinflation process and policy framework, particularly against a bac kdrop of renewed energy price pressures. In this note, we assess four key drivers of the TRY outlook: inflation and monetary credibility, the current account balance, FX reserve accumulation, and the political backdrop. ORTHODOX STABILIZATION The TRY continues to weaken against the USD in an orderly and largely predictable manner, with depreciation increasingly reflecting inflation differentials rather than concerns over policy. High carry, tight monetary policy, and sustained portfolio inflows have helped contain volatility, although the eventual easing cycle will provide an important test of investor confidence. records.text: set of the Strait of Hormuz closure, India's gold imports declined sharply in 2Q'26, falling 51% q/q in value terms and 48% q/q in volume terms. The weakness largely reflects a normalization from the record 2.54moz ( ~$12bn) of gold imports in January 2026, as well as the 15% import duty hike in May 2026, which weighed on import demand and inventory accumulation. India's seasonal gold demand typically peaks in 4Q, with imports generally rising after June and building through November. However, higher import duties and increased recycling are likely to temper the seasonal recovery in 2026. Negative local premiums, averaging -1.6% in August 2026 and -0.9% MTD in September, following -1.2% in July, point to weaker import demand. Assuming August and September imports match July 2026 levels, and imports during the remainder of 2026 follow normal seasonality in line with 2025, total imports would reach 15.7moz, implying a 5% YoY decline. However, we expect imports to rebound in 1Q27 post SOH resolution in 4Q26 and likely import duty reversal in 1Q27. These results suggest that low reported economic sentiment likely reflects a n more fundamental, downbeat assessment of the state of the world rather than the economy. Consumer sentiment may therefore not improve for the foreseeable future even if the economy continues to outperform and, as a result, will likely remain a less useful tool for predicting economic dynamics. Consumer sentiment fell sharply in 2020 and remains depressed despite solid economic fundamentals, including a healthy labor market, a booming stock market, and solid consumer spending and GDP growth. To illustrate the risks to inflation from natural gas prices, we consider here various scenarios ( Exhibit 49 ). Our current baseline inflation path is based on the market-based forwards for natural gas using the average of ten trading days per 31-August (see here). From that, one scenario is based on the latest forecast by our commodity strategists ( Exhibit 20 ), with a peak close to €90/MWh in 4Q26. Based on their view that risks remain to the upside, we consider an alternative with even higher prices, peaking at €100/MWh. And to span a wider set of outcomes, we also consider a path where the recent price uptick reverses and we drop back to levels around €50/MWh during the winter months with further downside through 2027. In the upside scenario headline inflation could stay above 2%Y until 4Q27, while the downside scenario would see headline below 2%Y in mid-27: Exhibit 50 shows the alternative paths for headline inflation across the three scenarios compared to our baseline. Across all paths the divergence from our baseline is most notable during 2027, as gas prices tend to affect consumer prices with some lags (see here for a summary view of transmission across countries and background to institutional factors driving that). Based on these factors, fair value for the current 10y/20y term-premium curve is currently 77bp, around 4bp above the latest actual level of 73bp, indicating that current valuations are somewhat rich. The decline in the 20y JGB term premium from early-month levels may also reflect a lower OIS term premium as expectations for BoJ rate hikes have increased. Accordingly, if Governor Ueda's press conference after the September meeting is viewed as dovish, renewed behind-the- curve concerns could put upward pressure on the 20y JGB term premium. The Nikkei QUICK survey showed 1.75% as the most common terminal-rate forecast (Nikkei, 10 September), while the 2y1m forward OIS is near 2.3%. Even discounting the forward OIS pricing of the term- premium component, market pricing for BoJ hikes may be somewhat excessive relative to economists' forecasts. Market-implied probabilities of a large hiking cycle are now quite extreme in major DM rates markets and ratio payer spreads on the LHS look attractive. In swap spreads, the environment continues to be spread-positive but longer-term risks remain. Options: Are markets getting ahead of themselves? Evidence is now building that a global developed market rate hiking cycle has started. The Fed and ECB have both raised rates, and while the BoE hasn't yet, at today's meeting a significant fraction of the MPC thought that a hike was appropriate. Markets have moved to assigning a meaningful probability to renewed hiking cycles. But an important message from this week’s meetings is that beyond their next moves, central banks' paths remain much more conditional than markets are expecting them to be. The market has been assigning a lot of weight to energy prices as the principal impetus for hikes, and the outlook for energy prices is genuinely unpredictable. However, the reaction functions outlined by the Fed, ECB and BoE depend on more than just the direct effect of energy on headline inflation. In our view, policymakers are much more concerned about underlying core inflation, labor market tightness and how anchored inflation expectations are. How RN resolves those tensions, may depend on the margin of Marine Le Pen’s victory, if she wins. A very large victory in the Presidential election, especially if flowed by a large victory in the legislative election, would in our view equip her with personal legitimacy, which would allow her to carry out more redistributive “old- RN” policies. By contrast, a smaller margin of victory in both elections would force her to compromise more with the more liberal, fiscally conservative “new RN” and with the priorities of her conservative allies (led by Nice mayor Eric Ciotti). So in practice, we do not have a 2 x 2 but a 3 x 2 matrix of plausible policy outcomes. Differences between the secondary branches of the decision tree (whether the government has a majority in Parliament) may paradoxically be more important than differences between the primary branches (who is President), especially for the domestic topic likely to be of most interest to investors: the fiscal trajectory. records.text: Metal Matters 11 September 2026 Citi Research 2 India's gold imports improved in July on a sequential basis but remained below historical levels. The month-on-month recovery was largely driven by a rebound in gold jewelry exports, which increased refiner/exporter demand for imported gold. In contrast, the year-on-year decline reflects the combined impact of higher gold prices, elevated import duties, and a weaker rupee. In June, the IBJA noted that exporters faced problems in sourcing gold over GST applicability (The Economic Times, 22nd July 26) at the import level may have slowed down imports. Following the May 2026 duty increase, domestic gold premiums turned negative at -2%, as traders liquidated inventories accumulated prior to the duty hike and deferred fresh purchases in anticipation of a potential rollback in duties. As gold prices fell in June, this destocking cycle largely came to an end, while investment demand began to recover. Reflecting this shift, gold ETF inflows totaled $525mn during June and July compared to outflows in May. At the same time, the market witnessed a notable increase in old jewelry exchanged and, more importantly, sold outright for cash. Kalyan Jewellers said its old gold for cash share increased to double digits (Indian Jeweller, 27th Aug 26) in 2Q’26 from single digits previously. The market is therefore allowing investors to sell rate outcomes materially above the Fed’s projected path while still retaining a wide range over which the structure makes money. Arguably, the distributions appear more extreme in Europe and the UK. That said, the vol markets in EUR and UK are likely more fragile than in the US, and the appetite to sell vol is likely low given the underperformance of vol selling in these markets ( Figure 2). We therefore recommend buying a USD 6m1y 1x1.5 payer ATM vs ATM+24 spread at near zero net premium. The trade retains exposure to further Fed tightening while selling outcomes that require the hiking cycle to extend materially beyond the median FOMC path. The median transaction multiple of 9.5x is therefore a more representative reference point. What have 2004, 2015, 2022 and now likely 2026 got in common? They are the only years this century that have seen the start of a US rate hiking cycle. The only caveat being whether a rate hike actually happens and, if so, whether it marks the start of a cycle or proves to be a “one and done”. Our economists now expect three hikes (this week, December and March – see their FOMC preview here), which I think just about qualifies as a hiking cycle. records.text: Box 1: Methodological caveats – AI-related exports vs. Tech exports In this report we estimate the growth contribution from tech exports—including consumer electronics for example—as opposed to solely AI-related exports. The reason for this choice is that the two inputs required by our method – deflators and domestic value-added ratios – are generally not available at the level of granularity needed to estimate real (volume) contributions for the most detailed goods categories. For example, the finest electronics category in OECD inter-country input-output tables is C26 Computer, Electronic and Optical Products, whereas export price indices are generally published at product-group level. With that caveat noted, the majority of recent tech export growth appears AI-related. Exhibit 6 shows how much of each economy’s tech exports are AI hardware. We defined broad tech exports (the noisier series) at the HS2/HS4 level that matches the sectoral granularity of price indices and inter-country input-output tables, and AI hardware (the signal) at HS6 using definitions adopted in IMF’s World Economic Outlook Update. This share is high for Korea and Taiwan, and lower for Vietnam and Thailand, where broader non-AI electronics dilute the aggregate. It conceptually explains why tech contribution might be a better proxy for AI contribution in the former than in the latter. On this front, we think that investors are telling policy makers that they need to raise rates. And while Warsh’s J ackson Hole speech veered into the guidance camp, Figure 6 shows that investors have become increasingly convinced that a rate hike is needed. In particular, while the market raised nominals across the curve in response to Jackson Hole , it was concentrated at the short end, with real yields driving the change. Warsh effectively opened the doors to rate hikes and investors adjusted the policy sensitive part of the curve to that possibility. Since then, rates have continued to rise across the curve, with higher real yields dominating the moves at the long end. There is a Bessent factor in these recent moves, although crowding out from higher capital demands is inherent in Treasury’s buyback plans. Given economic resilience in the face of rising energy prices, this message cannot be ignored and may be the market’s most powerful message at the moment. In particular, Figure 7 show that real yields did not behave as they normally would in response to last year’s cutting cycle. The recent rise would also normally correspond to a period of policy tightening, with capital expenditures putting upward pressure on both capital costs and the inflation profile. records.text: Semiconductor margin expansion A sharp increase in profit margins for many semiconductor companies has contributed to the above-trend recent pace of S&P 500 earnings growth. The combination of strong demand and limited supply has boosted semiconductor prices and gross margins, with the most pronounced margin expansion among memory stocks. S&P 500 memory firms currently enjoy gross margins of roughly 80%, more than double their historical average. Across the semiconductor industry, gross margins sit at their highest level in decades, and consensus expects margins to remain at similar levels through 2028. Margin expansion has accounted for a large share of recent semiconductor earnings growth, but that boost should fade going forward. We estimate that about 1/4 of S&P 500 Semiconductor earnings growth in 2026 is being driven by gross margin expansion. Our equity analysts believe the balance of memory supply and demand is likely to remain tight through 2027, with incremental supply additions unlikely to impact industry margins until 2028 at the earliest. records.text: 2Q’26 from single digits previously. In August, reports suggest old-gold-for-cash transactions have increased to around 20% of jewelry business, as per Indian Jeweller. Higher recycling volumes, combined with elevated import duties and rupee weakness, have impacted imported gold despite the recovery in end-user demand. Consequently, while July imports recovered, they remained below last year's levels. The combination of strong scrap availability, trader inventory liquidation, and policy-induced headwinds to imports continues to weigh on gold import demand. Policymakers appear cognizant of precious metals-related outflow risks. Recent silver import restrictions, aimed at curbing such outflows, were partially relaxed after local premiums rose to ~ 7% (30-day MA, ex-duty), highlighting the unintended consequences of supply-side constraints. A similar approach to gold would likely be counterproductive, as tighter import curbs could widen local premiums and incentivize smuggling. Instead, authorities are reportedly considering a revamped Gold Monetisation Scheme that would, for the first time, allow jewelers to act as collection partners and earn incentives of up to 1% on mobilized gold, strengthening efforts to channel idle household gold into the formal supply chain. As such, a renewed monetization push appears more probable than further import restrictions, helping expand domestic supply and reduce import dependence. Our elasticities suggest that a (permanent) increase in TTF prices of 10€/MWh adds around 30bp to headline inflation over two years and reduces GDP by around 10bp, reflecting both direct and indirect impacts. Also in the ECB's assessment high energy prices tilt the balance of risks to the upside for inflation and to the downside for growth (see here). And the Governing Council raised concerns that elevated natural gas prices would pose risks to further strength in core inflation and could have a persisting impact (see here). Hence, in our view, if natural gas prices remain elevated for longer, this could lead the ECB to raise rates further. The next opportunity to review the stance will likely be in December (see our ECB Review here). At the same time, electronic trading has nearly doubled since 2023, from 10% to 19% of volumes – improving liquidity at the margin, even as block trades remain offline. The equitification of European credit: Rise of the odd lots Odd lots now dominate European credit trading – 80% of PT volumes and 64% of RFQs – well above the 50% seen in voice. Their rise pulls less liquid bonds into circulation but leaves dealers with harder-to-recycle positions. Faster turnover, netting and ETFs help manage this growing odd-lot inventory. List trading protocols dominate flows. Liquidity gaps remain, but they should narrow as volumes grow and symbiosis with the ETF ecosystem strengthens. records.text: M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 27 Autos Javier Martinez, Shaqeal Kirunda Energy price spikes tend to present downside for the Automotive value chain. A rise in energy prices, such as that caused by the current Middle East conflict, is broadly negative for the automotive value chain, affecting OEMs, suppliers, and tyre manufacturers through multiple interconnected channels. Although energy costs tend to represent just ~3% of overall OEM inputs, higher energy prices feed directly into inflation, raising input costs across the board, including raw materials, manufacturing energy, and freight. At the same time, elevated freight and logistics costs, alongside potential physical supply disruptions, increase operational risk and working capital requirements for suppliers and OEMs. These inflationary pressures also tend to keep interest rates higher for longer, which reduces consumer disposable income and weakens demand for new vehicles, particularly in cyclical segments such as passenger cars and trucks. For tyre manufacturers, this dynamic is compounded by higher oil-linked raw material costs (e.g., synthetic rubber, carbon black), while for OEMs and upstream suppliers, it translates into both margin pressure and softer end-market demand. Overall, an energy price headwind creates a negative demand and cost squeeze across the automotive ecosystem, delaying recovery and reinforcing cyclical weakness. records.text: ntrast in monetary policy constituted BoJ behind-the-curve premium. BoJ risk premium: We would like to show how such slow BoJ risk premium has been built into the JGB yields. In Figure 3, we allocate a cumulative rise in yield in 10y, 30y and 2y over the past BoJ rate hike intervals. It is clear that 10y and 30y yields rose most during 2025 when the BoJ paused hiking, while 2y yields rose basically in line with policy rate. But since the hike in December 2025, the incremental rise in yield has become smaller even if the absolute level reached the psychological milestones of 3% for 10y and 4% for 30y. Therefore, as the interval between BoJ hikes becomes shorter, such as three months going forward, we think that a further rise in yield is likely to become limited. For example, during the first week of September, the third sell-off after May 2026 met with a short cover rally as 2y1y, a proxy for BoJ’s terminal rate, rose (Figure 4).. records.text: e cost implications for consumers. While past experience suggests the scale of policy intervention is often more limited than expected, we recognise that media headline risks regarding intervention policies can weigh on exposed stocks. We therefore see intervention risk as largely country specific. We see UK policy risk as overpriced, see UK: Focus on Fundamentals.15th June, and with attractive entry points for SSE & NG, and note the UK already has an electricity generation windfall tax. Italy has proposed a 'gas price' cap on merchant power which, if confirmed, could weigh on stocks with hydro generation. While Spain has no measures currently, we note the country did intervene in 2022-24. The French electoral cycle could result in a heightened focus on energy pricing and affordability. Meanwhile, Germany historically has been less inclined to intervene in energy markets. However, we would also highlight that the likely short-term impact of high gas & power prices could be isolated to winter 2026/27 given the next wave of LNG supply coming online from end 2026. Continuing the trend observed since the beginning of the Middle East conflict, developments in gas and electricity inflation remained highly heterogeneous across euro area countries (Figure 6). Analysis Meats and delivery services provide the clearest contemporaneous read-through, as the relevant CPI and PPI categories measure closely related products or services. The vehicle relationships are less direct, but may reflect upstream production costs and common manufacturing conditions. The shelter relationships are better interpreted as broader housing signals. Concrete reflects construction costs and activity, while OER measures the rental value of the existing housing stock. The correlation therefore likely reflects shared housing market conditions, rather than concrete prices feeding directly into shelter CPI. More broadly, this exercise demonstrates the limits of relying on correlation alone. Inevitably, we include some categories without a direct connection that moved together historically. records.text: M Idea 84 Utilities National Grid (NG/ LN, NGG US) Sarah Lester Rating: Overweight; Price Target: GBP 14.75/sh (Upside to PT: 30%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: National Grid presents an attractive, high quality, low risk 10% 3yr EPS CAGR (MSe) which combines with a >4% dividend yield for a very nice >14% TSR. This is a necessary capex driven growth story. Not only does this growth span continents – National Grid owns and operates assets in the US and the UK – but this capex programme is also expected to span decades. It is a genuine, new growth paradigm for the sub-sector and we see this as undervalued in shares. Secondary AI capex winners/Broader idiosyncratic drivers: Whilst National Grid, as a power network business, could be seen as an AI capex play, what we view as most compelling is that actually, the near to medium term capex needs are not directly related to AI. In fact, it is a necessary capex growth driven story with critical investment in infrastructure to ultimately help customers (e.g. UK electricity transmission capex to lower constraint costs for the UK customer, or the safety importance of replacing leak prone pipes in the US). Given a stable labor market, many officials who might be on the fence about hiking can still support the move as a kind of “risk management” hike that will have only a modest effect on the economy and can always be unwound if and when inflation moves lower or the unemployment rate rises. However, to forge a consensus Warsh would likely be expected by his committee to explain in the press conference that this week’s hike is more of a “calibration” and should not be read-through to a series of further hawkish policy actions. He could potentially communicate this as consistent with his preference for limited guidance and a meeting-by-meeting approach to policymaking. Hiking with relatively dovish messaging could help Warsh achieve a unanimous vote in favor of a hike. NY Fed President Williams did not appear to be leaning toward a hike in recent comments, but left options open and might be willing to support the Chair in this case. Given the differences across the committee as many as two dissents in favor of holding policy rates steady would not be surprising. Updates to the summary of economic projections for Q4 2026 should be on balance dovish. The unemployment rate should be nudged 0.1-0.2pp lower and real GDP growth left about where it was in June at 2.2%. Potential candidates like former PM Gabriel Attal already stretch the timeline for reaching a 3% deficit into the 2030s, beyond the 2029 target that was agreed with the EU Commission. The RN on the other hand has only recently started to take a more fiscally conservative line. The envisaged balancing of current expenditure and revenues is for now largely unsubstantiated, and whether it would be achieved through spending cuts or after all revenue measures depends, as we hinted earlier, which version of the RN prevails in campaign and office. Without a clear mandate to take expenditure cuts to levels distinctly felt by a significant part of the electorate, we think it remains a plausible outcome that deficit reduction will only proceed gradually even in the case where executive and legislative bodies are in agreement. Beyond simple cuts, progress would depend on picking up the structural reform baton again. Amidst much negative sentiment, it’s sometimes unnoticed that some of the labour market reforms throughout the 2010s appear to be bearing fruit, a topic we addressed in more detail in a recent note. However, as structural economic reforms are concerned, the in-tray of the next government remains significant. A new proposal for an overhaul of the pension system tops the to-do list

records.text: M Europe Insight 32 Apparel Retail Grace Smalley & Cedric Norest Higher gas and energy prices are a negative for Apparel Retail, primarily through pressure on consumer purchasing power and discretionary demand. For many households, fuel and household energy are effectively non-discretionary, so a sharp price increase leaves less income for discretionary categories such as apparel and footwear. Lower-income brackets are hit hardest. As Chris Kempczinski (McDonald's Chairman and CEO) put it on the Q1 26 earnings call (early May 2026): "Clearly, when you have elevated gas prices, which is the core issue that I think we're all seeing about in the press right now, gas prices, inflation on that, that is going to disproportionately impact low-income consumers". There is also a direct cost impact: higher energy prices add to opex inflation through store utilities and logistics, although the effect is typically smaller than the demand-side impact given energy represents a relatively limited share of the apparel retail cost base. For apparel specifically, the pressure can come through both lower purchasing power and weaker store traffic. On Wednesday, the FOMC will deliver its policy decision in the US, where markets are currently pricing an 86% probability of a 25 basis point rate hike. Therefore, the key focus will be on the post-meeting forward guidance rather than the decision itself. Additionally, the Bank of Japan (BoJ) is expected to hike rates on Friday, while the Bank of England (BoE) is expected to keep the UK policy rate on hold on Thursday. Alongside these central bank decisions, we must continue to monitor developments in the Middle East. In summary: inflation, inflation, inflation. This will likely remain the defining theme for the remainder of the year. Our flagship quant portfolio is well-positioned for this environment, but it remains vulnerable in the short term to a sudden shift from inflation to recession. The upcoming central bank announcements and geopolitical developments in the Middle East will remain our primary focus. With that, we complete today's edition of Quant Pulse. Recent polling indicates a narrow margin between the two, with their difference falling within the margin of error in a second-round runoff. Of the 11 other candidates, four are polling at least 2% of voting intentions: three centrists, Augusto Cury (Avante), Ronaldo Caiado (PSD) and Romeu Zema (Novo), and one on the right, Renan Santos (Missão). Why this matters: The fiscal plan presented by the next president will likely drive changes in economic expectations and market reactions. Though neither has disclosed detailed plans, the winning candidate, whether Lula or Bolsonaro, will probably propose adjustments to the fiscal framework shortly after the election to set rules to help meet the fiscal target of a primary surplus of 0.5% of GDP by the end of 2027. As a result, policymakers are likely to monitor whether increased fiscal activity can stabilise the economy in September, in our view. Increasing probability of fresh fiscal stimulus : China’s tepid GDP growth raises the probability of fresh fiscal stimulus in Q4, we think. If economic growth fails to recover in September despite greater support from existing fiscal measures and the resulting real GDP falls to about 4.0% in Q3, we would expect policymakers to introduce fresh stimulus in October. However, given the narrow gap between underlying momentum and the annual GDP target, any fresh stimulus is likely to be delivered in a measured fashion. As fiscal policy is the most effective lever to counter short-term downward pressure on growth, we expect fresh stimulus to include additional RMB500bn in special LGB quota and/or more new policy-based financial instruments. In recent years, 30y yield/equity correlation tends to decline and turn negative when yields move sharply higher. Short-dated vol could pullback amid gradual rate hike Even though today’s above consensus CPI print might be enough for the FOMC to hike next week, the relatively benign details, including the muted shelter and medical care components, likely would not cause the Fed to deviate from their slow and cautious approach. As we have argued over the past few months, it is the pace that really matters if the Fed ultimately hikes. A cautious Fed that is not pressured to act aggressively and beat the forwards should keep short-dated vol anchored in the near-term even if they do hike gradually. Hence, we maintain our bearish gamma bias on the premise that the benign CPI details would not be enough to justify an immediate follow-through even if the Fed hikes next week. However, we believe the medium-term economic and policy uncertainties should continue to be supportive of longer expiries and a steeper vol term structure. records.text: ab 14 September 2026 Global Research Canada Economic Perspectives August CPI in line, BoC deliberations up next Headline inflation fell -0.1% over the month on a non-seasonally adjusted basis in August with the annual rate holding at 3.0%. Core CPI, excluding energy and food, was flat over the month in August, versus the 0.4% rise in July, but faster than August last year, pushing the annual rate of core CPI up 0.2pp to 2.1%. The Bank of Canada's (BoC) preferred inflation measures both held at prior rates, with the weighted-median measure at 2.0% in August and the trimmed-mean measure at 1.9%. Core inflation remains around 2%, price pressures seem concentrated in components directly impacted by energy prices, rather than demand driven. The breadth of price increases looks contained but the share rising more than 3% on an annual basis did rise in August. The weighted share of components rising within the 1-3% band on an annual basis was 32.4% in August, 37.0% in July, while the share rising faster than 3% rose to 36.9% in August from 33.9% in July. We continue to expect the BoC to remain on hold for the remainder of the year but as we noted in our preview, the risk of hikes is rising after the focus on "too high" inflation in the September meeting communications. records.text: FX hedging design of the benchmark portfolio. As per the finalized rule, the maximum allocation to unhedged foreign currency-denominated debt instruments is set at 100% for fund stages 1–4, 50% for stage 5, and 20% for stages 6–10. Our estimate for total foreign currency debt comprises DM and EM fixed income, plus an assumed 50% of total high-yield fixed income to account for its foreign-currency portion, resulting in a minimum required FX hedge of USD 9–13bn. This figure is notably lower than our estimated current AFP hedging volume of approximately USD30bn. Consequently, AFP's current hedging position is already aligned with this requirement, meaning it does not act as a binding constraint on their FX hedging activity. We believe the more critical factor for AFPs is the benchmark portfolio's hedging design, under which foreign investment-grade fixed income is 100% hedged; for foreign high-yield and emerging market fixed income, the benchmark requires a 100% currency hedge for participants aged 50 and older (stages 5–10), whereas the benchmark for affiliates under 50 remains unhedged. Based on this logic, the estimated FX hedging amount ranges from USD17-25bn.

records.text: ince March's unanimous hold, dissenting votes have steadily increased, highlighting growing divisions within the committee. Governor Bailey has maintained a neutral stance, albeit with a dovish tilt, placing him in the middle of the pack of the members we track. A vote for a hold from him remains all but certain given that he has continued to push back against hikes, most notab ly at Jackson Hole. Nevertheless, he has increasingly flagged the upside risks to inflation, potentially narrowing the gap between his current stance and support for future hikes. Deputy Governor Lombardelli could be the wildcard this time round. She has kept a relatively low profile since the July meeting, and her post -meeting rhetoric surprised on the dovish side despite a history of leaning hawkish. While we expect her to remain in the hold camp, she could yet join the dissenters, continuing the recent trend towards a more divided MPC. Chief Economist Pill, the original dissenter, continues to lead the hike effort, consistently ranking as the MPC's most hawkish member in the media coverage . He has remained vocal on inflation risks and repeatedly expressed discomfort with the current wait -and-see approach favored by the majority. That said, he has stopped short of advocating a full hiking cycle, instead arguing that policy should remain an "active choice", which pushes back on intensifying market expectations. August imports are likely to remain weak amid negative local premiums, shifting demand to later months. Seasonal demand should support imports during September-November, while December typically sees post-festive moderation. Higher import duties discouraging inventory buildup, with traders importing against immediate demand. Expectations of potential duty cuts ( Moneycontrol, 27-Aug-26) are delaying stocking. India's gold import spending reached ~$38bn in Jan-Jul 2026, versus $21bn in the same period of 2025. Matching last year's import volumes would lift 2026 gold import expenditure to $70-78bn, assuming average gold prices of $4,000- 5,000/oz. This would imply an additional $11-19bn of dollar outflows relative to 2025, increasing pressure on India's balance of payments and FX reserves. Such an outcome appears inconsistent with recent policy trends, as authorities have historically raised import duties to curb gold imports during periods of FX reserve pressure. Consequently, the macroeconomic and policy backdrop suggests India is unlikely to match 2025 gold import volumes. records.text: Global bond yields have risen sharply YTD, driven by stronger nominal growth, n lingering inflation, fiscal concerns and increased competition for capital from AI. This follows the large bond sell-off in 2022. As a result, the past 5 years have been among the worst periods for bond investors in a century, although yields have only returned to long-run historical averages rather than exceptionally high levels. Are bonds becoming more attractive again for multi-asset portfolios? The n optimal bond weight in a balanced portfolio will be conditioned by (1) relative return, (2) relative risk, (3) diversification benefits and (4) the return on cash. Higher yields improve carry and prospective buy-and-hold returns; they also provide a larger cushion against further yield increases and thus lower risk. However, the return relative to equities will be driven mostly by equities, n especially in the near term. And more inflation volatility, fiscal risks and less negative equity/bond correlations suggest that duration may provide less reliable protection than before the COVID-19 crisis. Finally, while bond term premia have picked up, they remain relatively low in a long-run context, lowering the incentive to increase duration. We see a case for a return to more ‘normal’ strategic bond allocations but the n tactical case for adding long-dated bonds is mixed. records.text: M Idea 10 Exhibit 6: EUR has traded in line with energy over the past six months Source: Bloomberg, Morgan Stanley Research That relationship is somewhat counterintuitive. Oil's USD denomination mechanically biases its relationship with EUR/USD positively, but Europe remains a large net importer of energy. Historically, rising higher energy prices have represented a deterioration in the region's terms of trade, a drag on real incomes and growth, and therefore a headwind for EUR especially when energy price movements result from fluctuations in global supply mediated by conflict. In other words, an increase in energy prices associated with geopolitical risk in the Middle East would normally be expected to support the USD and vice versa. We think the recent EUR-energy price relationship is best understood through a perceived asymmetry in central bank reaction functions. Higher natural gas prices have raised Euro Area inflation expectations much more than US inflation expectations. One-year US inflation swaps are around 2.6%, not far from February 2026 levels, while equivalent Euro Area inflation swaps are around 3.5%, roughly 175bp above their February levels.

records.text: While there are several plausible explanations for the US population becoming more downbeat, the timing aligns with a perceived deterioration in societal and government institutions. The share of GSS respondents with “a great deal” of confidence has fallen for nearly all institutions since 2016 (left chart, Exhibit 5), with medicine and science, the military, education, and the Supreme Court seeing the largest declines. While the declining confidence in US institutions is arguably a continuation of a long-run trend, it has increasingly correlated with lower happiness since 2020. To illustrate the strengthening relationship between declining institutional trust and happiness, we use the detailed survey microdata to construct an aggregate institutional distrust measure across the 13 institutions that respondents are asked about in the GSS. We then regress binary indicators of whether a respondent self-identified as being on this “institutional trust” proxy and use the regression results to decompose the happiness gap. The results of this analysis are shown in the right chart of Exhibit 5. We find that relative to historical averages, the decline in institutional trust explains a disproportionate amount of the decline in net happiness over the last few years. In contrast, the change in respondents’ perceived financial situations had a much smaller effect. QT: Endgame September's QT decision was expected to be relatively routine, with the MPC widely anticipated to authorise a £50bn reduction in its gilt portfolio, with £31bn of passive reduction and £19bn of active selling. Instead, the Bank outlined a multiyear model of reduction that will see it run down the APF gilt book to zero by 2034. The main details are: • The Bank will run down its £488bn gilt portfolio at an annual average pace of £46bn by the• end of 2034 via annual sales of £20bn plus maturing bonds. • APF gilt holdings of bonds maturing by December 2034 will not be sold and held to• maturity (£222bn). • APF bonds maturing after December 2048 will be held to maturity as an asset backing current• and future note supply (£120bn). This is a return to the 2005-08 balance sheet structure. • APF gilts maturing between 2035 and 2049 (£146bn) will be sold to the DMO, not the market.• Operational details will be announced in April 2027. Apple attributed all of its recent gross margin compression to higher memory costs, which they expect to persist over the near term. Exhibit 7 shows the optimal bond weight and portfolio Sharpe ratio at different equity/bond correlation levels.2 With higher equity/bond correlations the optimal bond weight decreases, and that means lower Sharpe ratios and higher portfolio volatility. The optimal bond allocation also decreases with better relative equity returns vs. bonds (Exhibit 8) and higher relative risk (Exhibit 9). records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 September 2026 ab 10 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research Recent data and near-term forecast PCE inflation in August and upcoming months Based on the August CPI, PPI, and import prices, we project headline PCE prices increased 0.32% in August and core PCE prices increased 0.27%. There is considerably larger uncertainty surrounding these translations than usual. Methodological changes to software, legal services, and portfolio management services will be introduced at the same time that the August PCE price data is released on September 30, and the BEA has released only partial information on these methodological revisions. Historical revisions will also be published on September 30 that include updated source data as well as the methodological changes back to January 2021. As a result our projection of 12-month headline and core PCE price inflation has a considerably larger standard error than the front month. In the most recent release through July headline PCE price inflation was 3.70% and core PCE price inflation was 3.34%. We expect the August numbers will show headline PCE price inflation around 3.57% and core PCE price inflation around 3.18%. While these are notable downward shifts from the most recent release, we expect that ex post 3.18% will look like no progress on core PCE price inflation since early 2024. Unlike in the US, where the Fed is likely to hike twice this year into a world of strong aggregate revenue and capex growth, the ECB has already hiked twice into 0% €IG revenue growth & negative €IG capex growth, with a slight recovery in margins being driven by cost-cutting rather than any fundamental business improvements. A third ECB hike by year-end, coupled with the latest spike in commodity prices, is only going to make existing macro headwinds worse. As our recession indicator highlights, European economic downturn risks remain at average to slightly above average levels, and are bouncing around with commodity prices, as economy-wide profits (from the European national accounts) remain very sensitive to underlying inflation, particularly in a world of subdued pricing power. In addition, €-spec-grade credit metrics are turning in the wrong direction, with worsening net downgrade rates and default rate counts over the last 9 months, completely diverging from the improvements being seen in the US (Figure 10 & Figure 11). Coupled with a more hawkish ECB outlook, that is why we expect European spec-grade default rates to remain stuck near current levels at 4.5% through the Q2’27. records.text: M Europe Insight 18 Aerospace and Defence Ross Law, Marie-Ange Riggio, Leonore Pele Overall view. We see Aerospace & Defence as relatively resilient to higher European gas prices. Direct gas expenditure is generally small relative to labour and purchased components. The more important transmission channels are electricity, energy-intensive materials and processes (particularly castings, forgings, heat treatment and specialty metals) and the financial health and delivery performance of lower-tier suppliers. Cost exposure to gas. Low, and lower than in 2022. Direct energy accounts for a low single-digit percentage of total cost and is unlikely to be a major earnings driver for most A&D companies. Exposure is predominantly indirect through electricity-intensive manufacturing and the cost of aluminium, titanium, nickel, forgings, castings and other purchased components. As an example, Airbus consumed ~1.06TWh of natural gas in 2025, against total company energy consumption of 3.89TWh. Applying the increase from the €36/MWh average European wholesale gas price in 2025 to the current €79/MWh price to all of Airbus’s reported consumption would produce a gross, unhedged annualised cost increase of approximately €47m. This would be equivalent to only ~6bp of 2025 revenue and ~70bp of adjusted EBIT.
