While no longer arguing for an outright ‘Frexit’ , animosity towards the EU, its institutions and policies is still part and parcel of the party’s DNA. Rates Strategy View: a pre-election trading plan for OATs — Summer supply and the early polls for the 2027 presidential election have taken OATs to cheaper levels. For now, the price action is likely driven by who is most likely to face Le Pen in the run-off. Budget talks add to widening risk, but OAT net supply is light to year-end. Any further widening is likely modest in the near-term. Early next year, there could be 5-10bp of tightening in OAT-Bund should the centrists unite. Then, as the election nears, it would be primarily about the chance of Le Pen winning. At this point, we suspect OATs will trade cheaper than BTPs by 10-15bp. Equity Strategy — We expect French political risks to remain a source of volatility into the presidential election. French equities tend to be more volatile than peers around key elections and have historically underperformed ahead of the event, while wider sovereign spreads have weighed disproportionately on Financials and other domestically exposed sectors. Our models suggest French equity valuations relative to the overall European market have already embedded more political risk premium

Active ETFs are not just a conversion story Active ETF AUM growth may overstate the liquidity impact on underlying bonds, as a meaningful portion of that growth reflects a change in investment wrapper rather than genuinely new demand for fixed income exposure. While mutual-fund-to-ETF conversions, the introduction of ETF share classes and a degree of cannibalisation from traditional mutual funds have all contributed to active ETF growth, our analysis suggests these factors alone are unlikely to explain the full expansion of the market. For example, mutual-fund-to-ETF conversions have accelerated in recent years. According to FUSE Research, 68 firms completed 202 conversions (in both fixed income and equities) between 2021 and February 2026, representing c. $263bn in AUM and attracting $38.6bn of net inflows in 2025 alone (Figure 15). While notable, this converted AUM remains small relative to the overall size of the active ETF market, suggesting that conversions alone are unlikely to account for the market growth. FIGURE 15. Given past experience with coalition talks, a new government is usually in place within one to two months, but there have also been exceptions like the record 4.5 months after the 2018 election. The Autumn Budget, usually due in September, will likely be delayed this year until the government is formed; if this takes longer than mid-November, the outgoing government can act as caretaker and submit a budget bill. Campaign themes: Economy vs. migration and security The 2026 election campaign was dominated by economic topics as well as the future of Sweden's migration policy. Concerns addressed by all parties were household finances, jobs and growth; welfare; defence; crime and prevention; integration; and climate and energy. Among these, the opposition focused in particular on unemployment, the cost of living and subdued economic conditions, while the Tidö parties campaigned on migration, integration and law-and-order themes as key issues. records.text: European Multi-Asset 14 September 2026 Citi Research 8 The international focus on fiscal risk adds to the asymmetric bias for OATs and could upscale widening. Context always matters. A challenge for OATs is the coincidence of domestic political risk with a global focus on fiscal vulnerabilities amid a bearish bond environment stemming from high inflation and resilient growth. While much of the recent attention has been on the UST long-end, fiscal issues in Europe are arguably harder to solve given lower growth potential and significant spending pressure (not least from defence). The French presidential election may provide the latest example that there is little political and public appetite to take fiscal pain. There is also repatriation risk from Japan, although flow data suggests there has already been a significant reduction in OAT holdings. The extent of further OAT underperformance in the near-term likely depends on who looks most likely to face Le Pen in the run-off. With 7 months still to run until the election, our aim for now is to focus more on the buildup phase rather what the outcome might mean for OATs (which will also depend heavily on legislative elections that will likely follow in June 2027). However, the two are clearly highly connected as the market adjusts to polling. A series of rate hikes would be much more meaningful for that pickup, and in turn money fund inflows. With the next hike most likely not coming until December (see our economists' Fed call here), any turnaround in flows from higher yields is probably more of a 2027 story. That means it is unlikely to affect flows any time soon, leaving the underlying tepid trend a potential risk for money fund flows over the near term. We estimate that Treasury is set to issue about $240bn in net bills to private investors in October and another $160bn in November ( Figure 3 and Figure 4). Money funds are the largest buyers of T-bills, and with more supply on deck, bill yields may need to cheapen to incentivize funds to absorb that issuance. And absent inflows, that would mean reducing allocations elsewhere, such as in repo or agencies. In other words, money funds absorbing the next wave of bill issuance becomes incrementally more challenging, given this underlying trend. A useful guide to how funds may reallocate is the shift in portfolio composition during July and August, when Treasury issued roughly $500bn of bills to private investors ( Figure 5). Money funds absorbed almost all of that supply, purchasing around $450bn of bills

records.text: We Expect a 6-3 Vote for a Hold with Risks of a 5-4 Given limited signs of second-round effects and the latest commentary from Bailey, the MPC looks set to hold Bank Rate at 3.75% at the September meeting. We expect another 6-3 vote split. Pill, Greene, and Mann are all likely to continue to support a 25bp hike given the further increase in energy price pressures. Our baseline is that the remaining Committee members continue to favour a hold, but there is some risk that Lombardelli could join the dissenters. While she said that her decision to support a hold in July was not a close call, her paragraph also signalled that she could respond to risks of second-round effects stemming from persistently higher energy prices. Communications Likely to Note Rising Upside Risks We expect the communications to acknowledge an intensification of upside risks to the inflation outlook since the last meeting given increased energy price pressures. At the same time, we think that the Committee will continue to note that there are few signs of second-round effects so far. records.text: 1. There are two themes dominating our investor conversations: the impact of AI and the rise in interest rates. The two issues are linked as demand for capital from both the private and public sectors increase. In the private sector a surge in capex spending to fund AI infrastructure has eaten into free cash flow and forced companies to raise more in debt and equity markets. Meanwhile, government borrowing needs have increased as priorities shift towards upgrading critical infrastructure, energy security and defense at a time when cyclical inflationary pressures driven by higher energy prices are also resulting in higher policy rates. The combination has pushed up the cost of capital. As recently as 2022, for example, 30-year bond yields in Germany and Japan were close to zero (Exhibit 1). A rise in yields, together with more uncertainty (over geopolitics and the future impact of AI) have, in combination, pushed up the cost of capital. 2. This rise in yields comes after a near-record period of equity outperformance relative to bonds over 10-year holding periods (Exhibit 2). records.text: At the same time, 1yf 2y UST yields are already close to 5%. In other words, the forward curve is already pricing something close to inversion. That appears difficult to reconcile with a scenario in which the Fed is merely recalibrating policy modestly around neutral. Historically, sustained curve inversion has been associated with more aggressive tightening cycles, such as in 1994, 2000 and 2022, rather than episodes like 1997, when the Fed delivered a limited adjustment and subsequently remained on hold. We therefore favor curve steepeners, with our preferred expression being the 1yf 2s10s SOFR curve. The main risk is a renewed escalation in the Iran conflict that drives energy prices materially higher and forces markets to price a more aggressive policy path. Even in that scenario, the forward-starting nature of the trade should help limit downside relative to a spot steepener. records.text: Relatively low rates volatility allows for selective overlay hedges for bond portfolios to improve near-term risk vs. latent convexity. Rates receiver swaptions on shorter-dated rates can provide a more convex hedge for a recession, with central banks likely to remain very responsive (Exhibit 25). With front-end forward rates having increased strongly YTD but rates volatility being somewhat anchored, the entry point for front-end receiver swaptions appears attractive. This is both due to the central bank put in the event of growth risks but also near-term potential rates relief in the event of lower energy prices – during previous recessions, a receiver swaption on short-dated rates offered higher payoffs than S&P 500 OTM puts (based on current pricing). On the flip side, 3m put options on longer-dated bonds (TLT) could help protect fixed income portfolios that have already more duration risk – higher 30-year yields allow investors to better fund put protection strategies (Exhibit 26). Long curve vol expressions can hedge against the more extreme growth/policy tails. Excluding the volatile semi-durables category, underlying momentum in core goods inflation strengthened further in August, with the three-month moving average m/m SAAR rising to 3.2% (+0.4pp from July). This extends the acceleration underway since the turn of the year, leaving underlying core goods inflation momentum running several multiples above its 2025 pace (Figure 10). For now, price pressures remain concentrated in a relatively narrow set of categories, notably healthcare products, largely reflecting developments in Germany, and information and communication equipment (Figure 12). We still see little compelling evidence that higher energy costs are feeding through to consumer goods prices. However, we expect the inflationary effects of the Middle East conflict to become increasingly visible. records.text: wed monetization push appears more probable than further import restrictions, helping expand domestic supply and reduce import dependence. GMS 2.0 (Economic times , Aug 26), if jeweler-led and structurally reformed, could unlock India's ~ 25,000-tonne idle household gold stock (Hindustan Times, Sep 26) – a strategic lever to reduce import dependency, ease current account deficit, and create a formal domestic gold supply chain. India is evaluating GMS 2.0, shifting from a bank-led model to a jeweler-led model, leveraging their grassroots reach and consumer trust. The original 2015 scheme failed – only mobilizing a negligible fraction of idle household gold – due to cumbersome KYC norms, low interest incentives, and poor awareness. Under the revamp, jewelers become primary collection points, assaying gold and channeling it into the formal system, improving accessibility in Tier 2/3 markets. With India importing ~800–900 tonnes annually – a key driver of the current account deficit – monetizing dormant holdings could meaningfully cut import demand and forex outflows. This would boost domestic gold supply liquidity, dampening local price premiums over LBMA benchmarks and offering jewelers a cheaper alternative to imported bullion. Success hinges on resolving purity certification trust, capital gains tax clarity, and jeweler compliance, without which participation remains tokenistic. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: If capex were fully expensed, consensus 2027 S&P 500 EPS would be 22% lower than under current accounting rules. The current gap between actual reported and hypothetical fully-expensed earnings is one of the widest in recent decades, exceeded only as earnings fell more quickly than capex during the recessions of 2001 and 2008. Hyperscaler capex has consistently surprised relative to consensus estimates during the last few years, and the potential for additional surprises going forward creates a wide range of potential S&P 500 earnings outcomes. Our equity analysts expect hyperscaler capex will total $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, in which case the current tailwind from AI capex to S&P 500 EPS will fade by 2028. Exhibit 10 below outlines upside and downside scenarios around that base case. Next year, a $250 billion surprise in hyperscaler capex — in either direction — would shift S&P 500 EPS growth by about 6 pp in the same direction. We estimate that hyperscaler capex would need to decline by roughly 30%, to $570 billion, to offset earnings growth for the rest of the S&P 500 in 2027. This decline would reduce earnings for the AI infrastructure complex by about 40%, leaving their profits about 25% above 2025 levels. Based on ~80 years of historical analysis, there is an inverted "U" relationship between the 10yr bond yield and S&P 500 multiples. The relationship is positive up until an inflection point, which is a function of the earnings growth backdrop. During periods of above-trend EPS growth (~15% y/y), 10yr yields can continue to rise to ~5% before the equity multiple starts to de-rate. Currently, forward consensus EPS growth is calling for 20%+ and the S&P 500 is trading at ~18x on 2027 EPS. If these strong growth projections are realized, history suggests that the multiple not only has room to re-rate higher but that equities should be able to withstand a 10yr yield level closer to ~6%, see Figure 5P / E S e n s i t i v i t y t o R i s i n g Y i e l d s - B y E P S G r o w t h R e g i m e . Indicators of trend inflation suggest it is closer to core CPI than core PCE  As we noted last month core CPI inflation and core PCE price inflation are showing considerably different inflation pictures. Those divergent patterns continued in the data released in the past month with core CPI inflation edging down to a new post-pandemic low and core PCE inflation holding at one of the highest levels in the past 2½ years. Which measure is a better indicator of the overall trend in inflation, and which measure will converge to the other, will be important for the path of interest rates and inflation-linked markets.  Overall, measures of trend inflation, as well as outside data from wages, inflation expectations, and other current drivers of inflation (AI adoption, crude oil price increases, tariff increases, and housing rents) all suggest trend inflation is likely below the elevated level of core PCE price inflation and is likely to decline further over next year or two. Not much slowing in inflation until December except for methodology changes  We project little decline in inflation between now and November data that is released in December across all inflation measures — except for the methodology changes to PCE prices that will be published in two weeks on Wednesday, September 30.  With CPI, PPI, and import prices in hand we project core PCE prices rose 0.27% in August

The earnings of the banks were boosted by sharply rising leverage and the asset that they were financing – US real estate – did experience a valuation bubble. When the housing market collapsed, pushing economies into recession, it triggered a sharp fall in underlying earnings for the banking sector. There are important differences today. First, technology profits remain very robust, and balance sheets are strong overall. Second, interest coverage ratios for the aggregate S&P 500 and its median stock, for example, rank in the 99th and 68th percentiles relative to the past 20 years. Third, demand for compute is accelerating and outstripping supply; Microsoft recently declared their intent to triple data centre capacity in 6 years. The bottlenecks are increasingly power, land and data centre capacity rather than a lack of compute demand. At our annual Communacopia Technology Conference, Nvidia reiterated its 2030 AI TAM outlook to $3tn-$4tn and supply constraints continue to be broad based. Nonetheless, any slowdown in profit growth, in an environment of a much higher cost of capital, could put downward pressure on equity prices, reducing confidence in future cash flows across the ecosystem from the hyperscalers to the ‘pick and shovels’ that have been benefiting from the capex boom. 10. records.text: Exports and Beyond—Asia’s Broadening AI Dividend Investment in the artificial intelligence buildout continues to grow, with a large fraction of spend (roughly 2/3 the value of a data center) ultimately going to equipment producers in Asia. Earlier this year, we estimated the impact of surging tech exports on GDP growth across a range of Asian economies. In this week’s Asia Economics Analyst, we update those estimates and also look at spillover effects on domestic demand, including investment (in manufacturing export capacity as well as local data centers), consumption (via estimated equity wealth effects), and government spending (on the back of large increases in exporter profits and thus corporate tax revenues). Exports – A growing AI capex impulse The global AI spending backdrop remains supportive for Asian tech exporters. Bloomberg consensus estimates for US hyperscaler capex continue to rise (Exhibit 1), and are now at $800bn in 2026 and $1.1tn in 2027. Stronger AI-related investment underpins our upward revisions to growth forecasts across Asian economies (Exhibit 2); most have reported stronger-than-expected Q2 GDP growth numbers. In August, officials in Korea, Taiwan and Singapore all revised up their 2026 growth forecasts, with stronger-than-expected AI demand cited among the supportive factors. Four elections, and they matter equally Most observers of French politics currently focus primarily, if not exclusively, on the Presidential elections, which will take place in two rounds on 18 April and 2 May 2027. This is understandable, but in our view is understates the complexity of the electoral process and the range of outcomes that may result. Presidential elections will take place at those dates because that is when the second term of President Macron expires. There are currently no other elections scheduled in 2027 because the term of the lower house of the French Parliament (National Assembly) runs until the late spring of 2029. In practice, however, it is certain that whoever is elected President in early May will rapidly use the Presidential prerogative, under the French Constitution, to dissolve the National Assembly and call for legislative elections. France is indeed a parliamentary democracy, where the ability of any government to deliver any policy agenda is conditional on the existence of a supportive majority in the National Assembly. Effectively, the government is appointed by the President, but it emanates from Parliament. It is customary for a newly elected President to seek to obtain a supportive majority in Parliament by convening legislative elections in the immediate aftermath of their victory. records.text: M Idea 36 Diversified Financials Adyen (ADYEN NA) Russell Quelch Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €1,300/sh (Upside to PT: 40%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: Despite rising competitive intensity in global payments, we believe concerns around Adyen’s ability to take share are overdone, with the company continuing to grow materially ahead of the market through a combination of share-of-wallet gains (which account for two-thirds of Adyen's growth algorithm) and geographic expansion. North America and APAC, which together represent 71% of the global payments TAM, remain significantly under penetrated (Adyen's expected market share at ~2.5-3%), providing a long runway for growth, with recent wins like Toast and OpenAI demonstrating the company's ability to expand in the US. We see point-of-sale as the next leg of the story, with in-person volumes already growing 28% YoY and our forecasts implying a 31% PoS volume CAGR over 2025-28e. We continue to expect rates to remain at 0% this year (while targeted FX purchases would likely be used against renewed CHF appreciation). That said, if the widening rate differential continues to lead to further CHF weakness, it should ultimately allow the SNB to start normalising policy. The expectation of more ECB rate hikes (we now expect the ECB to raise the depo rate to 2.75% in December) is likely to intensify the debate. We think the SNB will want to see sustained CHF weakness materialise before embarking on hikes, so that we expect lift-off only in mid-2027. However, in our view the risks are clearly tilted towards a hike already in March or December and more than one hike in 2027. Market pricing at the time of writing is for two hikes until June 2027. Key to watch will be Chairman Schlegel's speech at the SNB Watchers Conference on 5 November. We outlined a roadmap to SNB hikes and what to watch in our latest Switzerland quarterly. records.text: UK Utilities Peter Crampton Barclays, UK | Laura Marconi Barclays, UK What makes assets in your sector attractive today? As we pointed out here at the start of the Iran war, European utilities carry a structural advantage in the current commodity environment: They carry low direct exposure to Middle Eastern LNG, yet they own the infrastructure that becomes more valuable when global gas markets tighten. Their earnings are leveraged to higher gas and power price levels, volatility (trading) and the long-term repricing of security-of-supply premia. After more than a decade of flat-to-negative electricity demand, 2025 brought the inflection point, marking the first year in which multiple European countries reported power demand growth. Europe's power system is now contending with an unprecedented quadrilemma: decarbonisation, affordability, security of supply and, newly, demand growth, and the resolution of that stress runs through a multi-year build-out of flexible generation, storage and, critically, networks. Over the last 2 years, we have seen a capex supercycle emerge in power transmission networks across the continent. We expect this growth to run through the decade, with distribution capex growth likely to accelerate thereafter, as data centre demand outstrips the current pace of generation and grid build. records.text: Broadening AI dividend, though exports remain dominant We present the aggregate results of our estimates by economy in Exhibit 15. AI remains the principal growth driver for Korea and Taiwan in 2026, reflecting their central positions in the value chain. Among ASEAN economies, Malaysia appears best placed to benefit, with meaningful exposure across semiconductor assembly and testing as well as data centers. The rest of Asia is also positioned to gain, though to differing degrees and through different channels. Taken together, however, tech exports remain the dominant transmission channel through which the AI investment cycle supports regional activity. Most other spillovers typically only amount to a few tenths of a percentage point of GDP . This is economically intuitive, as they are downstream effects of export strength, with export-generated profits ultimately funding additional investment, fiscal revenue and consumption. This positioning is inherently double-edged. While the region is highly leveraged to the AI supply chain and has so far delivered robust growth thanks to the investment boom, such concentration leaves the region vulnerable to any reversal in AI investments. A moderation in hyperscaler capex, whether driven by higher financing costs, greater investor scrutiny of ROI or slower-than-expected progress in AI adoption, might generate a meaningful growth headwind for the region. records.text: M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 9 Energy: Historically Low European Gas Storage Levels Martijn Rats, Charlotte Firkins, Alice Winograd The outlook for the European gas market this winter has turned increasingly bullish in recent months. Ongoing tensions in the Middle East and slow summer storage builds in Europe have already driven a +150% rally in TTF (major European gas price benchmark) since late February, pushing prices to ~€80/MWh. However, we still see price risk skewed to the upside over the coming winter (MSe base case €85/MWh avg over winter, bull case €130/MWh avg) for the following reasons: • The window for the return of Qatari LNG before northern hemisphere winter has now effectively closed. Force majeure notices now extend to early November for EU buyers of Qatar LNG and early to mid October for Asian buyers. This removes the possibility of an autumn loosening of the LNG market that would have let Europe accelerate injections and enter the winter with healthier inventories. We now assume Qatari flows to Europe normalise only into Q1 27. • European gas storage entering winter will be at its lowest in the 15 years of European gas market data. Following the collapse in LNG imports over summer, we forecast pre-winter fill in our European perimeter of 71%, 5pp below the previous end-October low of 2021 and 20pp below the 10-year average. Valuation: On an EV-to-implied EBITDA basis using the backlog of already contracted projects, Subsea7 is still trading at a deep discount to US peer TechnipFMC and to historical (i.e. pre-2014) levels (Exhibit 50 ). Exposure to energy shortage risk (from ongoing SoH disruption)? On a standalone basis, Subsea7 is not materially exposed to the Middle East and should be a net beneficiary of a relocation of resources into other regions over the coming years. However, Saipem is particularly exposed to the region (~40% of backlog), and a longer disruption period poses near-term earnings downgrade risks for the company. records.text: | Resilient, but also fragile: Growth has surprised us to the upside in Italy in 1H26. While we remain cautious on growth ahead in Italy, we revise up by 20bp our growth forecasts in 2026 and 10bp in 2027 on the back of a mark to market from a stronger 1H26. We now see GDP at 0.7%Y in 2026 and 0.4%Y in 2027. Three items have been performing better than we would have anticipated: private consumption, exports and investment in non-residential construction activity - see Exhibit 33 . Private consumption, worst is yet to come: While compensation per employee growth has returned to pre-pandemic levels, still solid and above our expectations employment growth is allowing overall compensation to support private consumption. The other half of the picture is a lower than expected saving rate. Data for 2Q26 saving rate are not yet available, but income and consumption data point to a saving rate falling below pre- pandemic levels - see Exhibit 34 . That would make Italy the only country amongst the euro area big four to see such a low saving rate, vs pre-pandemic standards. We think that the decline in saving rate might be an initial reaction of households to higher inflation. With real compensation per employee growth in negative territory again in 2Q26, we think it is a matter of time with inflation staying at these levels, before consumption will adjust accordingly. We hence expect a correction in private consumption in 2H26.

For these reasons we see greater than usual interest from financial investors in airlines that have relatively modern fleets and strong aircraft order books. Short-haul airlines are typically more attractive than long-haul airlines, since narrow body aircraft are more of a commodity than long-haul aircraft, whose on-board products vary widely. Long-haul aircraft are expensive to transfer between airlines and the assets are thus less fungible. The potential to acquire airlines at currently depressed valuations, with access to attractive fleets and order books, is particularly attractive to investors with aircraft leasing businesses, as they can look to rotate the fleets of acquired airlines into their lease portfolio, maintaining the airline as an ongoing business, but securing return on their investment by taking partial ownership of the fleet, leasing the aircraft back to the acquired airline and having the option to deploy future deliveries from the airlines order book either into the acquired airline or directly into its lease portfolio. This is an unusual confluence of events that supports this increased relevance of M&A: aircraft scarcity, relative low listed airline share prices and yet continued strong demand for new aircraft all shape the current situation. 16 September 2026 32 Barclays | European Equity Strategy

records.text: M Europe Insight Morgan Stanley Research 39 (see here). Could Trading Hub Europe (THE) be used to accelerate filling? Under the post- 2022 framework, THE can act as the backstop for storage filling. With approval from the BMWE and agreement of the Bundesnetzagentur, it can procure market- based filling instruments and, if these are insufficient, buy physical gas and inject it into storage. And there is a precedent for that from 2022. Amid the sharp reduction in Russian supplies, THE intervened directly in storage filling, and ultimately filled around 49 TWh. To finance these purchases, the federal government provided THE with a €15bn credit line through KfW (Germany’s state- owned development bank), backed by a federal guarantee. The costs were subsequently refinanced through a gas storage levy (‘Gasspeicherumlage’), which spread the costs across gas network users and gas customers. What would determine whether THE actually intervenes? Storage levels alone would not necessarily justify intervention. Policymakers would assess the broader supply-demand balance, including expected pipeline and LNG imports, infrastructure availability, demand and the winter outlook. This is why intervention by THE is currently rather unlikely unless that broader assessment changes. Could Germany reactivate coal-fired power plants if the gas balance became tight? Based on a global sample of 3k fixed income tickers. Source: Bloomberg, Barclays Research This likely reflects the differing objectives of active and passive management. Active managers seek to generate alpha through security selection and therefore concentrate portfolios in their highest-conviction ideas, whereas passive ETFs aim to replicate broad benchmarks that contain thousands, or even tens of thousands, of securities. For example, the Bloomberg US Aggregate Index includes roughly 14,000 bonds, the Bloomberg US Corporate Index nearly 9,000 bonds, and the Bloomberg Municipal Index more than 66,000 securities. As a result, passive funds typically require much broader portfolios to minimise tracking error, while active managers have greater flexibility to concentrate holdings. Liquidity implications of these more concentrated portfolios may vary across sectors and time. While active management provides greater flexibility, managers in corporate credit, municipals and MBS must balance the pursuit of alpha, which often resides in less-liquid securities, against the need to maintain sufficient liquidity to facilitate creations and redemptions. The exception is the July 2033, but that is because the APF's holdings are negligible (£270mn). Nonetheless, it is notable that the premium on the Sep-2034 is not as pronounced as we see in some of the other issues, so it should begin to richen over time. The decision not to hold any operations before the publication of the operating modalities of sales to the DMO next April effectively takes c.£10bn of gilt supply out of the market (ie, around half the expected £19bn of active selling, as October to April covers around half of the old 12m QT cycle), most of which will have been in this sector. 17 September 2026 31 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Not enough to break

records.text: ties. MarFA was launched 10 years ago today. The model’s uniqueness comes from combining co- integration theory with Principal Component Analysis. The benefit of the estimation process is that determinant variables of the market do not need to be defined – instead, they are extracted from the co-movement of assets by PCA. The model itself has remained unchanged since its initial launch, but the approach has had a lot of innovation over the past decade. These fall into three main categories: ▪ Expansion of coverage: Increasing from 75 assets originally to now over 400 ▪ New methods for connectivity: Our Quant Vault webpage, Bloomberg launchpads and API. ▪ Advanced analytics: Including processes for understanding the information contained within the principal component and incorporating momentum of the fair value in trading decisions using the Mann-Kendall test We provide details and links of these innovations on page 2. BNP Paribas MarFA is a core model in our Quant Trades of the Week process. On page 3 we discuss the performance of the models. MarFA Macro has delivered positive out-of-sample performance since launch, but less consistent performance in recent years, pointing to the need for further study to understand why. We also aim to explore enriching the trading strategy to combine signals across our models. I’ve added Mike – if you add more names here, please make sure to add the same names to the workflow job. records.text: ith inflation expectations near 2.5% over the coming year, implies a short- run nominal neutral rate closer to 4%. Against that benchmark, a 4.1% or 4.4% policy rate is only modestly restrictive. Financial conditions tell a similar story. Equities remain near their highs, credit spreads are tight, and Warsh himself noted that he would be hard-pressed to describe conditions as restrictive. The transmission mechanism also appears weaker than in prior cycles. Households and corporates remain locked into borrowing rates set when financing costs were much lower, fiscal policy is still running budget deficits near 6% of GDP , and AI-related capex appears to be considerably less rate-sensitive than traditional investment spending (see here). The risk of a hawkish policy mistake, one that meaningfully weakens the economy and generates a large duration rally, therefore appears relatively low. Instead, a higher-for-longer policy path may have the opposite effect. An economy that continues to absorb higher rates would encourage markets to reassess longer-run neutral rates higher over time. Figure 7 shows that investors are still discounting a neutral rate of only around 3.3% in 5yf 5y rates, a level that remains difficult to reconcile with the economy's demonstrated resilience. 17 September 2026 5 Barclays | Global Rates Weekly: Not enough to break

The APF's long holdings are concentrated in 2044-52 and 2054-60 maturities so it will be interesting to see if these bonds now become natural candidates for the DMO's tender programme. The selling of debt to the DMO rather than the market would require modest increases in gilt supply. However, in the context of a gross financing requirement of around £275-300bn, any increase likely would be comparatively limited. Of interest to the market will be whether any increase will be mirrored with an increase in bill supply (ie, a "twist" type outcome) or more evenly distributed across the curve. In the absence of any details, it is nigh on impossible to say what might happen. The DMO could effectively finance the gilts across the curve, but whether this comes in bills or shorts and mediums, it does not increase long conventional issuance and continues the trend of declining WAM of supply. It remains unclear what the DMO will do with its newly acquired gilts. Paragraph 44 of the September minutes obliquely alludes to the MPC discussing the DMO's "ability to retire bonds" , but this is something that would have to be done in consultation with the market, given the implications for market indices. All told, the Bank and DMO have created a very positive environment for long-dated gilt spreads and the long end of the curve by creating a genuine shortage of paper that is unlikely to be alleviated any time soon. 17 September 2026 32 Barclays | Global Rates We

A 60- 70pp draw is usual in a normal-to-cold winter, which raises the possibility of Europe reaching critically low storage levels. This is not only a regional issue. European storage determines how much LNG the region has to import over winter, as LNG is the only real source of supply flexibility if inventories fall short. Europe is a major marginal buyer, so a low storage position drives competition with Asia for cargoes and pushes up international prices. Expectations of a mild winter are the main reason our forecasts are not already more bullish. Consensus in the gas market is for milder than average European temperatures this winter on a strong El Niño phase. Heating accounts for 50% of European gas demand over winter, so milder weather delivers material demand savings. We model mild weather reducing demand in our perimeter by 4% versus winter 2025/26, which we treat as a 'normal' winter in a post-2022 market. On that path Europe still imports more LNG YoY but avoids drastic depletion, ending March at 26% fill. However, relying on weather for supply security is a risky bet. Forecasts are already skewed soft on demand, so the room for surprise is to the upside. We forecast winter 2026/27 TTF prices of €85/MWh on average. records.text: Managing duration risk and convexity in bond portfolios In the last 5 years, with rising bond yields and positive equity/bond correlations, reducing fixed income duration in multi-asset portfolios improved risk-adjusted returns (Exhibit 24). As we recently reiterated, in the coming years we believe investors need to maintain exposure to innovation, protect against inflation and improve risk mitigation in portfolios. Longer duration bonds tend to provide more convexity during recessions and large ‘risk off’ periods – for example, a 60/40 portfolio with US 10-year or 30-year bonds would have outperformed both when the Tech Bubble burst and during the GFC. However, as mentioned earlier, the potential for large declines in long-dated bond yields might be more limited in the next crisis, and near-term rates volatility could remain somewhat elevated. Our rates strategists see the largest potential for rates relief in the front end vs. forwards, pointing to positions in the belly of the yield curve – that said, those would offer less convexity. We see cuts at a quarterly pace to reach 3.25% in 2028Q2. Our terminal rate forecast is 25bp higher than our previous estimate, given that growth has recently been firmer than anticipated despite Bank Rate remaining elevated. We view the risks around our forecast as two-sided. On the one hand, a near-term drop in energy prices or a weakening the domestic data could convince the MPC to remain on hold. At the same time, a more sustained energy price shock than our strategists forecast could lead the MPC to raise Bank Rate further. The government sets minimum filling requirements; for 1 November, the current rules imply an average target of around 70% across German storage facilities. Commercial market participants remain responsible for procuring and storing the gas. What determines whether companies have an incentive to fill storage? A key factor is the spread between current and expected winter gas prices: companies compare the cost of buying and storing gas today with the expected value of having that gas available later. There is also a regulatory discipline. If booked storage capacity is not used sufficiently to support the required filling path, the unused capacity can be made available to Trading Hub Europe (THE) (Germany's gas market manager, which operates and balances Germany’s nationwide gas market), while the original user remains liable for fixed storage fees. In essence, it operates a “use it or lose it” mechanism (rather than eg using fines). How important is storage for Germany’s overall gas supply? Storage is an important seasonal buffer, particularly during periods of high winter demand, but it is only one component of the supply system. Germany also receives gas through pipelines and LNG terminals. Key Takeaways In addition to higher oil prices, European TTF gas prices are up over 150% YTD & likely face further increases, according to our commodity strategists, as European gas storage enters winter at its lowest level in 15 years of data. As with the start of the Iran conflict, market consensus is shifting towards the assumption that rising energy prices materially raise European earnings risks. Our in-depth analysis, in collaboration with 11 sector teams, points to an entirely different conclusion - most notably, far more prepared corporates vs 2022. Many 'exposed' sectors benefit from recent years' investments in energy efficiency, material hedging into winter, electricity contract PPAs, inflation clauses or price escalators in contracts, pricing power &/or a demonstrated ability to pass on price increases. Sectors such as CapGoods, A&D, & Autos have just a low- single digit direct exposure to energy as a %-age of costs. Meanwhile, large sectors like Energy, Utilities, Banks & parts of M&M (thermal coal, aluminium) skew to EPS upgrade risk on higher energy prices. records.text: BoE Preview—Holding in September , Hiking in November The period since the July MPC meeting has seen energy price pressures worsen materially. Front-end oil prices have continued to rebound, and near-term gas futures are now higher than the adverse scenario set out in the Monetary Policy Report. Rising energy prices pushed headline inflation slightly above the BoE’s projection in July. We expect next week’s August figures to show a larger overshoot. Fuel prices are likely to rise faster than the Bank’s estimates, and we also expect services inflation to be firmer than the MPR projection. That should result in headline inflation rising to 3.1%, three tenths above the Bank’s estimate. The activity data have remained resilient. Our tracking estimate suggests that GDP growth is likely to come in four tenths above the Bank’s forecast in Q3 after strong monthly figures for June and July. The broader dataset has also pointed to improving momentum, with our current activity indicator well into expansionary territory. But we view market pricing as hawkish But we would view any tightening as insurance/risk management, rather than driven by materially broadening price pressures. Any tightening is unlikely to be the start of a prolonged hiking cycle. So we do view market pricing of close to four hikes as excessive. We don’t think that we are in the adverse scenario of the BoE yet because that scenario assumes much greater persistence in energy prices in future years and materially higher second round effects (peak of 1pp). We don’t expect second round effects to be as material or price rises to be significantly broad based, given the limited evidence so far, a soft labour market backdrop and restrictive rates. Even Huw Pill (who has voted for a hike since April) has noted that the BoE could lift rates without kickstarting a prolonged and aggressive series of increases. So we don’t think rates will reach the peak of 4.75% (unless things materially worsen), which the optimal policy path under the adverse scenario points to and which markets are pricing. Market demand for Nokia's optical and IP products remains exceptionally strong, so the key is unlocking supply capacity. Nokia's capacity at its second San Jose fab is expected to ramp up in late 2026 and into 2027; and its test and packaging operations in Pennsylvania will see a 10x increase in capacity by the end of Q3. This, we believe, could imply a 2027 guidance in optical + IP higher (MSe +22%) than the 2026 target of 18-20%; and the mid-term revenue guidance for network infrastructure division as a whole of 6-8% CAGR could also be too conservative. Core AI capex beneficiaries: Nokia is a key beneficiary of data center expansion as its customers (hyperscalers) need upgraded networking equipment to move vast quantities of data between existing and new data centers. AI & Cloud revenues are relatively small at <10% of Group currently, but could reach ~30% by the end of the decade. Valuation: On our estimates, shares trade on 20x '27 PE and 16x '28 PE. records.text: 11 Large discrepancies between pollsters: In the 2006 elections, only three major institutes – CNT, Datafolha and Ibope – published polls of voter intentions for the presidential race. From the 2010 elections, Vox Populi and CNI had joined this group. In 2022, the field became more crowded, with 14 pollsters gauging how Brazilians would vote for president. With that context, we examine 12 polls that consistently released data throughout the 2022 election, aiming to assess their accuracy against the final results. In the first round, the two front-runners were generally mis-estimated, especially Jair Bolsonaro, whose support was repeatedly underestimated: his vote share in opinion polls was, on average, 3.6pp lower than the actual result. The largest discrepancies came from Ipes​pe, Quaest, and Datafolha, each undershooting Bolsonaro by about 7–8 pp. CNT and PoderData were the most accurate overall. In the second round, CNT again proved the most reliable, only 0.2pp off Lula’s winning vote share, followed closely by Paraná and Quaest (0.5pp and 0.8pp, respectively; see Figure 11). Samples can make the difference: We observe variations in virtually every characteristic of the samples — gender, age, region, and education (see Figures 13– 16 overleaf) – which is likely to bias a particular pollster’s results depending on the dominant traits of the surveyed population. records.text: Marvin Loh, Cayla Seder 14 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material FOMC preview: No time like the present Based on market pricing, investors appear fairly certain that the Fed will hike rates this week. In reality, we think there remains a great deal of disagreement on that outcome, amongst both investors and the FOMC. Given Warsh’s approach to guidance and communication, we will naturally enter an FOMC with greater 2-way optionality than we have seen over the past few decades. Therefore, “20 bps above midpoint” does not necessarily contain the same degree of investor confidence that it once did. We are however pricing 90% odds of a hike, a figure that has expanded since payrolls and CPI . Our view is that there will be a plurality within the FOMC that will weigh recent geopolitical events as a risk to reaching the Fed’s inflation goals, and approach policy from a risk management perspective. With growth remaining solid, few signs of labour weakness, and continued strong demand for capital, we expect that the FOMC will raise rates by 25 bps this week, while signalling another hike before year end. To be sure, Warsh is walking a credibility tightrope and disappointing the markets after his J ackson Hole speech risks losing control of the long end, at a time when Treasury’s interference in the market has added fuel to duration volatility. Marvin Loh, Cayla Seder September 16, 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material Sept FOMC: Rate hikes without a family fight The Fed hiked rates by 25 bps, tightening financial conditions for the first time since 2023. Put to rest now is Warsh’s willingness to address the long -overdrawn inflation overshoot, with 5+ years of above target prices a critical consideration in the committee’s unanimous decision. An additional hike to 4.125% is now forecast in the dots this year, which is then forecast to remain unchanged through 2028. The SEP forecast optimistically pontificates stronger growth, stable employment and a slow glide towards inflation targets, essentially showing little knock-on impact from hikes. We think that this will prove a battle ground for investors, with one camp believing the Fed just committed a policy mistake, while other will feel another 25bps will not prove enough, particularly given the strong economic background implied by the Fed’s outlook. Count us in the latter camp, with the need for additional tightening in early 2027 before the Fed feel comfortable that its inflation mandate is in fact satisfied. And while rate expectations are aggressive relative to the signal from the SEP, this will not preclude a hawkish response from investors, who must absorb Treasury’s increasingly desperate attempts to contain yields. For one, institutional investors remain constrained to a degree by investment mandates, with certain bond funds, for example, unable or unwilling to hold ETFs on account of them being considered 'equity' . The growth and ease of portfolio trading has also likely reduced the role that ETFs might otherwise have played in helping investors manage inflows and outflows. At least equally important is the lower level of retail participation. Relative to the US, Europe has a more fragmented retirement savings market, a smaller (albeit growing) role played by defined contribution pensions, and a less-developed self-directed investment ecosystem. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 79 Transportation IAG (IAG SQ) Axel Stasse Rating: Overweight; Price Target: €5.80/sh (Upside to PT: 19%) – Risk-reward overview Investment case: Global airline capacity growth is moderating, particularly across long- haul markets such as the North and South Atlantic, reinforcing pricing discipline and supporting margins - especially in premium cabins. This backdrop is favourable for IAG, given its industry-leading premium-seat mix, dominant position on the supply-constrained UK-North Atlantic corridor and resilient demand trends. Our positive stance is also supported by: (1) sequential improvement in RASK, (2) disciplined cost execution and favourable fuel hedging, which we believe could drive earnings upgrades vs. conservative guidance. (3) A robust balance sheet (0.5x gearing) providing downside protection and strategic flexibility, and (4) resilient free cash flow (MSe FY26: €2.7bn vs. management guidance of <€3bn), underpinning the sustainability of its €2bn shareholder return programme. As we see further upside to EPS from continued CASK ex-fuel outperformance and capital returns, it makes IAG our preferred way to gain exposure to structurally attractive long- haul profitability. This contrasts with the more challenging short-haul environment, where excess capacity, pricing pressure and macroeconomic uncertainty continue to weigh on earnings prospects. Annual QT Review Likely to See Pace of Stock Reduction Reduced to £50bn This meeting will also see the MPC make its annual decision on the pace of quantitative tightening (QT). Last year the Committee opted to reduce the stock by £70bn, with £49bn redemptions and £21bn of sales which were tilted towards short- and medium maturities. We expect sales to continue this year; recent communication from Bailey has stressed the importance of removing interest rate risk from the BoE’s balance sheet, Bank staff analysis continues to point to modest impacts on yields, and swap spreads are narrower than a year ago. That said, with yields at high levels and reserves showing signs of levelling off in recent months, we do not expect the Bank to accelerate the pace of sales. As such, with lower redemptions of around £31bn this year, we think that the pace of stock reduction will decline to £50bn. We expect the £19bn of sales to once again be split 40/40/20 between short/medium/long maturities. Metal Matters 11 September 2026 Citi Research 3 Higher gold prices are driving two structural trends in the Indian gold market: increased recycling of gold jewelry and greater monetization of gold holdings, either through collateralized borrowing or outright old-gold-for-cash transactions. While gold continues to serve its traditional role as a store of value and emergency funding source, particularly in rural India and among agricultural households, its use as a financing instrument is broadening. Small and medium enterprises, traders, freelancers, and professionals are increasingly leveraging gold to meet short-term funding needs, including inventory purchases, supplier payments, and working capital management. Meanwhile, elevated gold prices have accelerated jewelry recycling among traditional gold-owning households. The affordability challenge has become increasingly pronounced: a 50g gold purchase would have cost approximately US$3,570 in 2023 (excluding making charges and GST), equivalent to 1.4x India per capita income of US $2,592. By 2026, the same purchase would cost about US$8,020, or 2.9x the estimated per capita income of US$2,813. As a result, consumers are increasingly opting to exchange existing jewelry for new designs rather than make fresh purchases. Higher gold prices have also accelerated gold monetization. For July, our intervention tracker did not signal any significant activity. Since then: Inflation higher, CHF weaker, growth solid Since the June meeting, inflation has risen to 0.8% y/y in August, with the July/August average of 0.6% slightly below the SNB's forecast for Q3 (0.7%). The pick-up since February has been largely driven by energy, with domestic price pressures remaining subdued. Looking ahead, we are tracking inflation at 0.9% y/y for September and expect it to pick up moderately to 1.3% y/y by year-end, driven by base effects and a weaker CHF. Overall, we expect headline inflation to average 0.6% in 2026 (up 0.1pp from our prior forecast) and 0.7% in 2027/28 (SNB: 0.6%, 0.6%, 0.7% in 2026-28). Meanwhile, the real economy had a solid start to the year. GDP increased by an exceptional 1.5% q/q Q2 (adjusted for licensing income from international sports events), driven by pharma exports but also with robust underlying domestic demand. Unemployment at 3.1% in August was unchanged from the SNB's June meeting. Overall, a return to trend growth appears likely, but we believe improvement on the labour market will be needed for a sustainable growth recovery and higher domestic price pressures. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 16 September 2026 1 Germany: Risks around CDU leadership unlikely to derail fiscal policy OUR KEY VIEWS ▪ While politically significant, we expect limited change in Germany’s fiscal policy course even if the Christian Democrats’ poor performance in September’s state elections prompts the party to bring in a new chancellor. ▪ The bar remains high for reversing reforms such as the debt brake or a collapse of the coalition. ▪ We continue to expect Germany’s economy to grow in a cyclical upswing as the mix of fiscal spending and a push from the global AI buildout keeps supporting domestic demand and exports. The September state elections in eastern regions could spur a change in the national leadership of the Christian Democratic Union despite state governments having only limited direct influence on federal policies. Indeed, in 2005 , former Chancellor Gerhard Schröder triggered a vote of no confidence after his Social Democratic Party performed poorly in a state election. However, even if Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s leadership is challenged, we think snap national elections are unlikely, and a potential successor would likely continue a similar policy path while the economy starts to feel the benefit of fiscal expansion. records.text: Please refer to important information at the end of the report and MAR disclosures 15 September 2026 ‹#› Fiscal risk premium: The market has a long built a negative perception about Japan’s fiscal status since the early 2000s, when JGBs became the first G7 government bonds whose yield rose above swap rates (vs. Libor at that time). This perception has been magnified upon each fiscal event, such as fiscal measures over Covid in 2020-21, the LDP trying to regain popularity with spending after fundraising scandals in 2023-24, and most recently by the Takaichi government. The market has been skeptical since the inception of the Takaichi government and more so over the JPY370trn strategic investment plan and the consumption tax exemption on food planned for 2027-8. We agree that while the consumption tax issue is the biggest concern as it is hard to see that the government will find credible funding, we see the trend of the falling debt-to-GDP ratio as something good (Figure 5). Indeed, the improvement owes much to the impact from inflation and lower bond prices, but tax revenue has grown more than nominal GDP (Figure 6) even during the period of deflation in the 2010s, owing to the various built-in measures and small hikes, although the contribution from each measure is small. In the last 10 years, the rules for various tax allowances (inheritance, spouse, income, mortgage etc) have become stricter. records.text: 16 September 2026 Germany Schnappschuss Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG The crucial question, therefore, is whether the recent recovery in industrial activity will translate into higher employment. So far this year, Germany’s manufacturing sector has combined rising output with falling employment: a jobless recovery. In the PMI survey, this is reflected in a remarkable rebound in productivity (see Figure 1). Although German manufacturing has considerable potential for AI-driven productivity gains, we doubt that these are the main explanation at present. Instead, many companies still have spare capacity after years of labour hoarding and remain cautious about hiring. If capacity utilization continues to recover, however, employment should begin to stabilize in the coming months. In August, the employment component already improved markedly in both the PMI and ifo surveys. This matters for the government’s reform agenda. By the time of the crucial state election in North Rhine-Westphalia in April, an improvement in manufacturing employment could make the ‘de-industrialization’ narrative easier to rebut. A solid result in this pivotal state would, in turn, give the government more room to implement the structural reforms needed to restore Germany’s industrial competitiveness over the next decade. We are closing our MXN basis flattener (U26-2y vs. U26-10y) at 5bp, booking a loss of 5.5bp (USD110k). The long-end MXN basis has struggled to decline due to a resilient MXN supported by a robust US cyclical position through remittances and trade flows. While we anticipate that a potential MXN sell-off, prompted by Fed hikes, could benefit this position by compressing long-end MXN basis and flattening the curve, we have opted to close rather than roll our position. This decision is driven by the risk of seasonal upside pressure on long-end basis, which is likely to stem from increased local external debt issuance and the associated hedging flows to pay long-end basis. Consequently, we maintain a short MXNCOP position to express our relatively bearish outlook on the MXN rather than utilizing the MXN basis curve. To recap, we initiated this trade on 3 June to capture rising MXN cash demand; additionally, the position provides exposure to a stronger USDMXN and lower hedging activity, which could compress long-end basis (see EM rates: Entering an MXN basis flattener trade).

records.text: M Update 2 August CPI Bank of Canada Implications Canadian inflation was unchanged at 3.0%Y in August, and the composition remains consistent with an energy-driven overshoot rather than a broader inflation problem. CPI-trim held at 1.9%Y and CPI-median at 2.0%Y, while CPI excluding food and energy rose only modestly to 2.1%. Food inflation continued to cool after remaining elevated for much of the past year, shelter remained subdued, and the apparent acceleration in travel-related services largely reflected base effects rather than renewed sequential price pressure. Headline inflation remains above target because of energy, but there is still little evidence that the Middle East energy shock is feeding materially into underlying inflation. Energy prices rose 15.5%Y in August, down from 16.9% in July but still contributing just over 1ppt to headline inflation. Gasoline prices have moved broadly in line with global crude prices and could firm again in September. Core inflation remains contained. CPI-median was 2.0%Y and CPI-trim 1.9%Y in August, while their three-month annualized rates were around 2.2%. CPI excluding food and energy rose to 2.1%Y from 1.9% in July and its three-month annualized rate remained firmer at 3.6%, but the composition is less concerning than the aggregate suggests. The Federal Network Agency (‘Bundesnetzagentur’, Germany’s energy-network regulator) assesses security of supply based on the interaction of pipeline imports, storage, LNG imports, infrastructure and demand. This also makes comparisons with 2022 imperfect, as Germany’s gas sourcing options and flows have changed materially. What role does the government play? The government primarily sets the regulatory framework and storage targets; market participants remain responsible for securing gas. The Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) sets energy policy, including filling targets, while the Federal Network Agency monitors security of supply and oversees relevant market rules. The “use it or lose it” provisions on unused storage capacity provide an intermediate discipline before direct state-backed procurement is considered. Meanwhile, the term premium remains contained alongside market expectations of fiscal risks. This is supportive of our view that high quality equities remain a valuable inflation hedge over the intermediate-term; this also justifies an equity risk premium near zero, a view we have held since COVID ended the 36-year secular bull market in bonds and disinflationary trend. • Quality has been a winner around the first hike. The equal-weight Top 1000 has typically recovered to +9% by nine months after the first hike, while quality has outperformed across every window around the move, including+3% over three months and +5% over the following year. It's also worth noting that cyclicals and momentum both typically outperform post the first hike. As we recently wrote, ex post equity risk premia in the last few years have been unusually high. Higher and more volatile inflation, as well as rising government debt/GDP ratios and fiscal spending, have supported equities relative to bonds. And more recently the higher nominal growth backdrop, boosted by the AI capex boom and higher energy prices due to the Middle East war, added further upward pressure to bond yields, while equities had tailwinds from earnings growth. As a result, from a valuation perspective bonds now look increasingly attractive relative to equities (Exhibit 4). Finding the right balance — drivers of the optimal bond allocation Are bonds becoming more attractive again for multi-asset portfolios? This is where Markowitz’s Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT) can help by quantifying the trade-off between return and risk while incorporating diversification. As we wrote before, even over long horizons the efficient frontier varies materially over time not only due to changing macro conditions but also to different valuation starting points. Based on an efficient frontier since 1950 combining the S&P 500 and US 10-year bonds (Exhibit 5), the tangent portfolio was close to a 60/40 portfolio (with a bond weight of c.36%) – thus a 60/40 portfolio was near the optimal asset mix. As of July 2026, we estimate that approximately $400bn of global active fixed income ETF assets were invested in this category, or roughly 60% of the total (Figure 3). Investor demand tells a similar story: within the active ETF universe, fixed income has attracted a disproportionate share of recent flows, with active bond ETFs capturing 34% of trailing 12-month inflows, ahead of US equity categories (Figure 14). A new liquidity dynamic may be emerging As the shift from mutual funds to ETFs increasingly penetrates active fixed income, an important consideration is whether the ETF wrapper can improve liquidity in the underlying bond market. While we believe the long-term impact on liquidity is likely positive, our analysis suggests the effect today is considerably more muted than in passive fixed income ETFs, for four key reasons: 1. Active bond ETF growth is more than a conversion story. 2. Active bond ETFs account for 20% of ETF assets, but just 8% of volumes. 3. Active ETFs currently play a limited role in the corporate bond portfolio-trading ecosystem. 4. Elevated oil prices could also pressure airline customer economics, potentially weighing on flying hours and Civil Aerospace aftermarket activity. Overall, we view the disruption as a potential margin and macro headwind rather than a material operational constraint, although risks would increase should elevated energy prices persist. In 2025, approximately 524,000 companies reported positive income but around 60% of them paid no income tax. Within that group, 70% recorded deductions in excess of income, while the remainder carried forward losses from previous fiscal years. Income tax accounted for about 54% of total tax collection in 2025, so the base of the largest single revenue source is where the Ministry of Finance has concentrated its reform agenda . The Budget changes the rules governing the base rather than changing the rate : For companies with accruable income above MXN50m, deductions equal to or below 96.67% of accruable income are capped at 99% of those deductions, and deductions above that threshold are capped at 96.67% of income, with the non-deducted remainder carried forward over the following 20 years. Prior -year losses can be applied only up to 50% of taxable profit in each year, once the deduction cap has been applied, an d the carry-forward period is extended from 10 to 20 years. The cap on net interest deductions falls from 30% to 20% of adjusted taxable profit. In this scenario, the risk of Merz facing a leadership challenge would increase significantly, in our view. On the flip side, in the decades ending in the 1930s and 1940s, as well as around the GFC, the optimal portfolio had close to no equities. Up until the COVID-19 crisis the optimal asset mix was actually not 60/40 but more like 40/60, similar to a risk parity portfolio with larger allocations to bonds. And after the COVID-19 crisis the optimal portfolio shifted to 100% equities – most investors would have been better off mixing cash with equities based on their risk tolerance instead of a balanced portfolio. 1 These allocations should be interpreted as directional signals rather than portfolio recommendations. records.text: Intuitively, we find that sentiment has declined more and remained lower for lower-income (top left chart) and lower-wealth (top right chart) households. These patterns demonstrate that lower-socioeconomic households are disproportionately downbeat on the economy, consistent with narratives that that cost-of-living pressures and a K-shaped economy are weighing on sentiment. Less intuitively, we find that sentiment is lower for GenX and Baby Boomers than for Millennials and GenZ (bottom-left chart), a pattern that cuts against the common narrative that younger households disproportionately face sentiment headwinds from cost-of-living increases and AI-job-displacement (although it does align with longer-run trends showing that younger households are generally more optimistic on the economic outlook). Also on the less intuitive side, we find that sentiment is higher among social media users (bottom-right chart), and that this outperformance is robust after controlling for age effects (not shown). While academic research has found that social media usage has a negative effect on economic sentiment, this pattern suggests that the benefits from greater social engagement dominate any social media-induced headwinds. records.text: FIGURE 33. Summary of Barclays' UK sector analyst views Sector Summary Mid Cap Consumer Corporate activity has historically accelerated when listed valuations diverge from private market values, with many consumer and leisure businesses acquired around 9-10x EV/EBITDA. Weak consumer confidence and persistent UK equity outflows have depressed valuations across the sector. Attractive opportunities lie in businesses where valuations discount temporary operational issues rather than structural decline. We highlight CVS, Watches of Switzerland and Cranswick as examples of high-quality assets trading at attractive levels. Business Services The sector benefits from recurring B2B revenues, outsourced business models and valuable data assets. Experian and Rentokil stand out as trading materially below their historical valuation ranges. Experian offers a unique data platform with AI monetisation potential and strong cash generation, while Rentokil's valuation does not reflect improving US operations. records.text: Central scenarios Central bank meetings used to be fairly straightforward, especially at the Fed. Data and verbal guidance, only rarely delivered at the last minute and meant surprises at scheduled meetings were uncommon. That is no longer the case. Terms such as dovish hikes and hawkish holds have entered the lexicon, alongside mysterious articles citing central bank sources. As we outlined in April in Less talk, less guidance, but a billion prices, the Warsh Fed brings greater opacity and therefore more volatility. Even with interest rate markets pricing a 95% probability of a 25 basis point hike today, several outcomes remain possible. The first, in line with the economist consensus only a week ago, is no change. Yet, as we argued in No time like the present, this would deliver one of the largest dovish surprises in a decade and, against rising inflation pressures, immediately revive concerns about Fed credibility. Recent reporting on the Fed’s tone has also turned more hawkish, making a hold unlikely, though not impossible. Meeting immediate expectations with a hike, however, will only partly determine the market reaction. The statement, press conference and, for now, dot plot will determine whether the move is judged hawkish, dovish or neutral. One year rate expectations are already above 4.6%, while the July median dot for 2027 was only 3.6%. If markets view the ECB as more responsive than the Fed to the inflationary consequences of higher energy prices, the shock can support EUR through relative front- end rates. Warsh's communication may make that perceived asymmetry less pronounced. We think Warsh's September communication may begin to shift that perception. A market perception that the Fed will be more reactive than before to moves in energy prices may diminish the recent positive EUR/USD beta to energy prices, even if European inflation pricing remains more sensitive to the shock. The potential for energy prices to stay elevated may therefore increase USD-positive risks – the opposite of the recent correlation. We therefore see our energy strategy colleagues' forecast for 88 EUR/MwH TTF and 100 $/bbl Brent oil forecasts for year-end as providing tailwinds to the USD over time.

records.text: Valuing S&P 500 earnings Like our forecasts and consensus estimates, market pricing suggests investors anticipate a deceleration in earnings growth going forward. This is true both for the broad market and for AI infrastructure stocks. For example, the share prices of semiconductor stocks have historically mirrored the path of consensus EPS estimates, and the recent moderation of semiconductor returns has aligned with consensus estimates for decelerating growth in 2027 and 2028. The current S&P 500 P/E multiple signals an optimistic outlook but market skepticism regarding the sustainability of current profits. In addition to rising interest rates, an anticipated deceleration in earnings helps explain the recent decline in the S&P 500 forward P/E multiple. Along with macro factors like interest rates, the level of corporate profitability has helped explain the variation in S&P 500 valuation over time. Based on the historical relationship between S&P 500 ROE and P/E, the current S&P 500 ROE of 24% — a record high — would point to a forward 12-month P/E of over 21x against today’s macro backdrop. Given current inflation and interest rates, today’s S&P 500 multiple of 19x would be consistent with an ROE of roughly 22%, more than 200 bp below the current level but otherwise matching 2021 as the highest on record. Still, we see two likely explanations. First, Exhibit 10 shows that consumer spending on automotive fuels dropped materially in March, and more than observed for instance in 2022-23. Second, households entered the energy shock with solid balance sheets, as shown for instance by elevated saving rates (Exhibit 11 ). records.text: sentiment We assemble a panel of 48 EM EXD funds, and extract data from Bloomberg on their weekly returns from 2018 onwards, as this is the earliest period by which we have sufficient data to generate fund-level features. We use this returns data to construct a candidate set of sentiment indicators, including rolling estimates of average pairwise correlation, cross-sectional median beta to EM EXD, cross-sectional rank persistence, return synchronicity, cross-sectional skew, and a concentration ratio based on the effective dimensionality of the fund covariance matrix. Each candidate time series is Z- scored using their 52w mean and SD. Issuance data: helps track primary market sentiment The second source uses data on all new EM sovereign and non-sovereign hard-currency issues since 2014. For each deal, we collect the basic terms of issuance, including pricing date, issuer, maturity, issuer rating, issue size, and the spread at issue. This captures the quantity of new supply coming to market, the characteristics of the issuer, and the terms on which that supply is being placed. New-issue pricing richness / concession The hypothesis: new issues trade richer to peers vs history = spread widening This component captures how rich or cheap new issues are trading relative to comparable secondary-market spreads for the same broad rating and maturity bucket. In our data, higher spread-to-rating readings (meaning cheaper new issues or larger concessions) are associated with tighter future EM spreads. Periods when issuers had to offer wider concessions tended to leave better forward spread performance from that point. New issue pricing therefore enters the tracker with an inverted sign, so wider concessions push the tracker to forecast near-term spread tightening, while richer primary pricing makes it forecast near-term spread widening. records.text: e median fed funds rate projection rose 38bp for 2026 and 50bp for 2027, with both years now landing at 4.1%. Read in isolation, that looks like a committee turning more hawkish. Read against what else moved in the SEP , it looks more like a committee marking to stronger data. Figure 3 shows that the unemployment rate forecast for 2026 was revised down 20bp, to 4.1%. Core PCE inflation was revised up 10bp, to 3.4%. The committee's own estimate of the longer- run policy rate rose almost 20bp, from 3.06% to 3.25%. Feed those changes through a balanced Taylor rule (using a coefficient of 1.5 on both inflation and labor-market deviations), and it largely accounts for the increase in the median dots ( Figure 4 and Figure 5). If anything, the implied policy rate path for 2026 should have moved somewhat more. As a result, the increase in the dots does not appear to reflect a more hawkish reaction function. It largely reflects a stronger economy. The Fed's new inflation projections may actually create downside risk to the near-term policy path. The median participant forecasts core PCE inflation of 3.4% Q4/Q4 in 2026. Given the upcoming methodological revision, that already looks somewhat high. Chairman Warsh's own framing suggests the revision is worth roughly 10-20bp; he noted that y/y core PCE inflation in August was running at 3.2%, even though the current methodology points to something like 3.35%. According to the finalized rule, the maximum allocation to unhedged foreign currency-denominated debt instruments is set at 100% for fund stages 1–4, 50% for stage 5, and 20% for stages 6–10. Affordability pressures continue to build across large-ticket purchases, with mortgage rates, vehicle financing costs and still- elevated prices weighing on household purchasing power (see The burden of proof has shifted, 11-Sep-2026). Yet the labor market remains healthy, as the most recent data prints have shown. As a result, consumption appears to be slowing rather than stalling, even as investment increasingly accounts for a larger share of incremental growth. Looking ahead, we expect both CPI and PCE inflation to move lower through 2027 as energy-related price pressures fade, which should help stabilize real purchasing power. In our view, the result is an economy where investment remains the primary growth driver, while a resilient consumer helps sustain the expansion rather than detract from it. Macro is translating to earnings revisions that are notable not only for depth but also for breadth: 2026 and 2027 earnings revision breadth has remained well above its historical norm not only across Tech but also for multiple non-Tech sectors (including Financials, Healthcare and Discretionary, where revisions breadth is tracking above 10Y averages) and for the S&P 500 as a whole. records.text: European Multi-Asset 14 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Political elections, especially if too close to call, typically elicit interest from investors. Not all of them, however, carry meaningful implications for the economy or markets. From our perspective, political change only matters if it comes with policy change. Elections genuinely attract our interest if they are liable to result in (1) a change of direction of domestic economic policies, (2) a change in the ability of government to carry out policies, (3) a risk to political and social stability or (4) a break in relationships with the rest of the world with consequences for the latter. The French elections that will take place in the spring of 2027 are materially relevant on all four dimensions. In addition, their outcome is, in our view, very uncertain at the moment. We consider them therefore as a noteworthy risk event, not only for the French economy and market, but for Europe too. In this, note, we initiate what will be an ongoing coverage of the run up to the elections by providing a concise overview of the election process, a presentation of the main forces in presence, and a taxonomy of what we see as the main stakes from a market perspective. This is followed by contributions from Citi’s interest rate, equity and foreign exchange strategists on how they see each market being affected by the French political situation as it unfolds. 1.
