records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 September 2026 ab 32 US Economic Perspectives UBS Research Comparison to the forecast models As with most Phillips curve style models, our models were unable to forecast the inflation as it surged upward in 2021-2022 and, as expected, the majority of models were not a good guide as inflation has fallen. (Note that in the early part of 2022, the core PCE price inflation time-varying trend models and the component model remained above 4% throughout the forecast horizon, which at that point went through the end of 2024, compared to the 2.8% that has been published for 2024 inflation.) In particular, the models do not include an effect for changes in the mix of demand and the supply constraints that hampered efforts to satisfy this changing mix. We believe the combined effects of the changing demand mix and supply issues were far more important in driving the initial inflation surge in 2021 than were the standard Phillips curve driver of aggregate resource slack, though fiscal spending and monetary policy have likely accounted for a fair amount of the reason that inflation did not fall faster from that peak. The models now project core PCE inflation of 3.5% to 4.0% this year (compared to our 3.3% pre-revision baseline) and 2.7% to 3.7% next year (compared to our 2.45% baseline). Furthermore, August saw a clear shift towards direct financing as enterprises sought lower costs relative to bank loans . Corporate bond net issuance doubled year-on-year to RMB271.2bn, while new corporate equity financing grew 40.1% y/y to RMB63.9bn. While TSF outstanding and M2 growth slowed to 7.2% and 7.5% y/y, respectively, their continued alignment with nominal economic growth indicates to the PBoC that monetary conditions are adequately accommodative. Consequently, further easing in response to weak credit demand appears unlikely. Robust export performance: Despite lukewarm domestic demand, China’s exports maintained strong momentum in August, with the growth rate accelerating to 25% y/y. AI-related products remained the primary driver of this robust performance: integrated circuit shipments surged 129.8% y/y, while computer shipments rose 76.5% y/y. Combined, these two categories contributed about 19pp to overall export growth. Auto exports also performed well, increasing 43% y/y, driven by a 37.2% rise in export volume. In terms of direct impact every 10bps move in OATs would cause an immaterial mark-to- market impact on either TNAV or CET1 capital; we estimate ~0.1-0.2% and ~1-2bps respectively. This channel has been particularly important in the US IG and HY corporate bond markets, where ETF liquidity is particularly deep. For active ETFs, however, neither channel is currently as effective. In addition, most active ETFs rely on cash-based rather than in-kind C/R mechanisms. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 16 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material BoJ : From cadence to comms The challenges facing the BoJ have changed considerably since their last meeting on 31st July. In our prior preview of that meeting, BoJ: A crisis of cadence, we argued that their tightening cycle, while well flagged, required more urgency. That has now come in a rush. At the end of July, the next move from the central bank was not fully priced until December, with the chances of move as soon as September at just over 25%. records.text: Primer on active ETFs Active ETFs sit between passive ETFs and active mutual funds. Like active mutual funds, they rely on portfolio managers to make decisions on security selection, duration, sector allocation and credit exposure with the aim of outperforming a benchmark. Unlike passive ETFs, they are not designed to track an index and typically hold more concentrated portfolios reflecting managers' highest-conviction ideas. What makes active ETFs different from active mutual funds is the wrapper rather than the investment process. Active ETFs trade intraday on an exchange, can be bought and sold throughout the day, and benefit from the ETF creation-redemption mechanism. By contrast, mutual funds are transacted once daily at net asset value (NAV). In many cases, an active ETF and an active mutual fund can be managed by the same investment team and hold broadly similar portfolios. The combination of active management and the ETF wrapper has helped drive rapid growth in active fixed income ETFs. Investors gain access to manager skill and potential alpha generation while benefiting from the liquidity, transparency and operational simplicity associated with ETFs. records.text: Swap spreads The Fed delivered its first rate hike since 2023 in a unanimous 12-0 decision. The committee updated the SEP , which was more hawkish than expected, reflecting the underlying strength of the US economy, resilient labor market conditions, and still elevated inflation, while the hike was intended to support "a timelier return" to their 2% inflation goal (see here). The hawkish tone pushed front-end yields higher, flattening the curve, while breakevens fell. Against this backdrop, swap spreads were resilient and continued to show signs of strength after the Fed meeting. As rates have increased in recent months, particularly with the long-bond touching multi-decade highs, 30y spreads led the widening move. In fact, longer-tenor spreads have reversed much of their tightening in the first half and are closing Q3 on a strong note ( Figure 3). Increased long-end buybacks should do little to affect outright yields but should have more of a clean effect on relative value relationships such as spline errors and swap spreads. We continue to like being long the 10s20s30s ASW fly and find that historically the long- end buybacks have been concentrated in securities near the 20y point and a larger Treasury footprint there should support the sector (see here). The stand-out this year on the spread curve has been at the front-end (2y). records.text: UK Economics 14 September 2026 Citi Research 3 The landscape beyond September In November, the Bank will publish a new set of forecasts. They will likely show more resilience in activity and notably higher near-term inflation. Recent economic growth has been stronger than expected, and some MPC members acknowledged this in last week’s Parliamentary hearing. However, their tone was relatively dovish, perhaps so not to contradict themselves when – as City economists expect – they keep rates on hold on Thursday. However, since then the ONS released its figures on monthly GDP activity. The latest monthly activity figures have come in so strong that it would require a large contraction in the monthly GDP data in August and September – a cumulative 1.2% decline across those two months - to deliver the Bank of England’s current forecast of 1.1% growth in the year to Q3. T o give a scale of the adjustment needed, the month-on- month growth data for GVA hasn’t fallen this much since January 2021 (i.e. after Omicron). Yet that, in and of itself, is not a reason to hike rates. As we have been arguing since May, the pickup in growth is sectoral – driven by the white-collar sector, and in particular Information & Communication. This has also been matched with an increase in productivity growth—also because of ICT. records.text: US Economic Perspectives17 September 2026 ab 24 Box: Rules of thumb for impacts of key economic shocks We usually rely on estimated time-series models to bring in the impact of various factors on our forecast. However, rules of thumb are often useful to give a rough idea of how important a shock is likely to be. Below are a few key rules of thumb that we use:  1 percentage point increase in the unemployment rate pushes down core inflation by 15bp.  Permanent $10 per barrel level shift in the price of Brent crude pushes up the level of CPI by 40bp and core CPI by 4bp.  A one percent decline in the dollar increases consumer import prices by 0.15 percent.  A one percent increase in import prices results in a 0.12 percent increase in core consumer prices.  A one percent increase in CRB spot food index equals about 8bp in prices of food at home with about 2/3rds in the first six months and 1/3rd in the six months after that. (CPI food at home is 8% of the CPI basket.)

records.text: UK Life insurers, by contrast, screen somewhat richer relative to history, trading on low-teens forward earnings multiples versus a historical average in the high single digits, albeit while offering superior dividend yields relative to the broader European insurance sector. Stock implications Our preferred UK exposure remains Hiscox (OW). We view the company as possessing one of the most attractive standalone franchises in the sector through its combination of a leading specialty platform and a differentiated retail business. Retail represented approximately 53% of premiums and 48% of pre-tax profit in 2025, with management targeting double-digit growth by 2028, providing a level of growth diversification that many specialty peers lack. Hiscox's geographic footprint across the UK, US and international specialty markets would fit naturally within the broader consolidation trend. In May, UK trade press (Insurance Post) reported that Intact was exploring a potential bid for Hiscox (also see here), citing multiple sources at the British Insurance Brokers' Association (see Hiscox Ltd. / Intact: A credible tie-up strategically and cyclically, 15 May 2026). 16 September 2026 24 Barclays | European Equity Strategy

records.text: urrent oil and natural gas prices are very similar to the assumption in the Adverse scenario, but we think we are still far from the assumption of significant second round effects that were so critical to making inflation a persistent multi-year process in the Bank’s adverse outcome. To repeat, it’s only if these second round effects look likely to materialize that we think significant, sustained, policy tightening will be needed. In the November MPR, it is likely the Bank will disentangle their assumptions on the Adverse scenario. So far, that scenario incorporated both high energy prices and strong second round effects. However, plotting the inflationary path if only the high energy prices were to continue (with only limited feedback from second- rounds) would allow the MPC to argue that the inflationary effects on domestically generated inflation will be weaker than markets expect – justification for a lower rate path – despite higher energy prices. There have been occasions in the recent past when markets have priced in a strong sequence of BoE rate hikes. Something similar is happening now. When the MPC comes to discuss this shift in market pricing we suspect that they will draw on their analysis in Box F in the July MPR (Chart F.3). That box argued that much of the increase in market expectations for the path of Bank Rate between the start of the Middle East conflict and July was down to risk premia.
